I rise to a question of privilege. I wish to refer to a speech made in the house last Thursday by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght), at page 3695 of Hansard, in which he mentioned myself and the Union government and the Military Service Act. He based his remarks on a text book, Doctor Skelton's "Life of Sir Wilfrid Laurier." He said:
I am sorry the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) is not here, for the Toronto Globe referred to the widespread feeling of disappointment, while it is said that Mayor Church of Toronto stated:
"The Military Service Act will cost the country millions and is getting very little results. If the government had spent one-quarter of the money in voluntary recruiting, they would have got more men."
Let me say that this book does not quote the page or the issue of the Toronto Globe, nor does it say what I said, because the remarks were never made in that connection. I was complaining about one thing, and that was a lack of equitable enforcement of that act throughout Canada. I complained because before the act became effective Toronto and Ontario had been dried up of voluntary recruits, and hardly any could be further obtained.
I never saw Doctor Skelton's text book until this afternoon. And may I .say that the hon. member for Parry Sound has described the author of the book as an historian. Well, if he is an historian he should state facts. The book does not state facts, because the real fact is that from the start I strongly supported the Union government and the Military Service Act. My only complaint was in connection with the non-enforcement of the act elsewhere in the province, and particularly its enforcement in Toronto. I called attention to the fact that that enforcement was not equitable. In reply to the hon. member for Parry Sound I say that what I said was that the enforcement of the act was unfair to Toronto and to Ontario generally.

Two or three years before this war, from 1937 to 1939, I urged on many occasions here a compulsory selective service register for Canada. I have been a supporter of that policy, and before and during the 1940 election I supported conscription and the policy of equality of sacrifice. Then the hon. member for Parry Sound makes things worse by casting reflections upon me, and by attempting to show a worse side of the picture. Referring to me he said "that I had been misled by my absentee leader". I was not a member of the House of Commons between 1917 and 1921. And may I point out in passing that the absentee leader to whom he refers has two sons in England, and that the party he refers to polled nearly one-half of the total vote in the elections of 1940. I might have something to say about these matters in another debate, because the hon. member has not stated the facts exactly and the connection to which they relate. His facts are not correct, nor are those of the writer of the book. I may challenge this or discuss it at another time.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, June 23, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. L. Usley (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Tomorrow will be the seventy-fifth anniversary of the founding of this dominion-a long time in the life of an individual, but relatively short in the life of a nation. Only one other nation-the United States-has made such rapid strides in intellectual progress, political development, and material wealth in such a short period of time. So rapid has been our growth along all these lines, so certain has been our advancement, that we have been largely unconscious of our own development or of our strength. Yet on this seventy-fifth birthday of this nation we are literally standing on the edge of an abyss, and the whole future of civilization hangs in the balance. What a paradox!
What the end will be, no one can foresee. Dark days ahead-yes. But victory in the end is certain if we of the united nations will but gird our loins, put on the full armour of our strength, and pull our weight in the great task which lies before us.
In one respect at least this budget is the answer of the Canadian people to the challenge of the hour. Financial sacrifice-yes. But, after all, that is the least we can do. If you do not believe that, remember the casualty lists of 1917 and 1918, and try to visualize those of this year, next year, and every year until this war is won.
There was neither glamour nor high-sounding rhetoric nor political adornment in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) to which we listened on Tuesday last. But there were statements and assertions of an arresting nature at the close of the minister's address which I sincerely hope caught the ear of all the people of Canada, including, if I may say so, those in this house who, in the early days of the war, advocated a moderate contribution-a middle-of-the-road course-for Canada.
I have observed during a somewhat long and full life that if you want to get the immediate attention of an individual you have only to say or do something which affects him personally, something which will affect his pocket-book. We have this something here in this budget.
The tax proposals are not only substantial; they are crushingly severe, and will bring home to all of us, as perhaps nothing else could, "the critical gravity of recent events and the necessity of making a supreme effort", to use the words of the minister, not only during this present year but in each succeeding year in which this nation, along with those of the united nations, will be engaged in a struggle for survival.
The position which the minister portrayed in the concluding paragraphs of his address is exactly the position which I have tried, perhaps inadequately, to portray to the Canadian people from the very first session of this parliament. There have been times when I have been appalled, and have had a feeling of despair at the apathy of a large portion of our people. In the early stages of 1940 there was a feeling of complacency which, in my view, was engendered and fostered by the attitude of the administration itself. Fortunately that has been reversed, both in the minds of the administration and in the minds of our people.
Their complacency, their desires for "gain and ease and advantage"-again quoting the minister-from now on must be submerged in the nation's will to win. I only regret that in one particular feature the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has not shown that will to win which is so urgently needed. But I say this, that sooner or later-I hope not too late -he, going along with the more forthright members of his cabinet, will change his views and practise what he has so long preached- total war with total effort. We are now approaching full conscription of wealth, and soon, I trust, we will be practising, in fact as well as in theory, the total mobilization and use of all the resources of the nation.
To those of us who recall the budgets of Mr. Fielding, in the pre-war days, the budgets of Sir Thomas White, in the days of world war No. 1, or even the budgets after that war, this year's budget is a stern reminder that two world wars have changed our whole economy, as indeed they have changed t4ie lives of every one of us.
The consideration of ways and means should be one of the chief preoccupations of this House of Commons, and I regret exceedingly that the delivery of this budget has been delayed to this late date in the session. Here we were, late in the fifth month of the session,

in our history. The delay in its presentation is directly attributable to the anxiety of the Prime Minister to maintain his political position in the country and has been brought about largely by his determination to cariy through the farce of the plebiscite and his policy of appeasement. We have had almost a hundred speeches by hon. members opposite on the debate on the address, and at least seventy-five on this mobilization bill. On this question of delay, six of the twelve months of the calendar year have passed. Now, after six months, business executives, and more especially taxpayers in the lower income brackets, are being called upon to make tremendous adjustments in order to meet the strain occasioned by this budget. Six months of the calendar year have gone by, and to bring down these changes so late in the year does not give the taxpayer any opportunity to make a twelve months' adjustment, but compels him to carry out a twelve months' adjustment in the last six months of the year. That position is unfair, especially for the small salaried man who has to budget at the beginning of every year and who makes his commitments in the first part of the year. It reveals an attitude of indifference to the plight of the people who are called upon to pay this budget, and it is wholly reprehensible.
In the more than five months in which parliament has been in session, we have really dealt with only three of four important pieces of legislation-the billion dollar appropriation for Britain, the two billion dollar war appropriation bill, the wheat legislation, and the dominion-provincial agreements. All the rest of the time was wasted on the debate on the address, the perfectly useless and wasteful debate on the plebiscite bill, and still later, the debate on bill 80, amending the mobilization act-all three of which measures should have been disposed of in as many weeks.
No wonder the people of Canada look askance at this House of Commons and, in some quarters, express amazement at our performance 1

We have not sacrificed much-nothing like what the people of Britain have sacrificed; nothing like what I fear we shall have to sacrifice before this war is won. Let us face the future manfully and realistically. Let us tap the national income all along the line without fear or favour. Let everyone from the highest all the way down do his share. Only then shall we be able to face our conscience and each of us say to himself: I am doing and shall do my part if it takes the last dollar. The stake is worth it, my friends. That is the text and that is the spirit I offer to the Canadian people to-day.
When Canada entered this war in September,
1939,	our basic sources of revenue were customs duties, excise duties and taxes, including a sales tax of 8 per cent, and income tax on corporations and individuals. From these sources, in the fiscal year immediately preceding the war, we derived a total of 435 millions of dollars.
In the fiscal year ended March 31, 1941, we collected from those same basic sources a total of 1,359 millions of dollars, or more than three times as much. I think it is fair to add that we have had some new taxes not differing in principle or radically different in any degree, except in quantum, from the old taxes.
The ability of a country with a population of less than twelve millions to pay in taxation a total of nearly 1J billions of dollars- averaging, as it does, about $120 per capita- without undue hardship, is a tribute not only to our people but to the material resources of this country.
In making this vast contribution in cash to the national revenues, there have been some inequities and some inequalities. In particular, in the field of personal income taxation, there has not been equality of sacrifice. I emphasized this on a previous occasion. When in
1940,	and again in 1941, the rates on personal incomes were raised by the budgets of those years, I indicated the view I held that the taxes then imposed on such personal income were inequitable and lacked the element of equality of sacrifice.
I now wish to deal in some detail, if the house will bear with me, with the proposals of the Minister of Finance with respect to personal income tax.
In his personal income tax proposals the minister has had three major objectives in view. First is the curtailment of present excess purchasing power and the diversion of as large a proportion as possible of the national income to direct war purposes. The curtailment of existing purchasing power is neces-

sary to-day in order to curb the causes of inflation and in order to divert labour from the manufacture of unnecessary consumer goods to the manufacture of war materials or to the use of those materials in the armed forces.
So far as curbing the causes of inflation is concerned, it will be recognized that the existence of a price ceiling may prevent inflation, but I suggest that it does not strike at the causes of inflation and certainly does not prevent inequitable distribution of available essential consumer goods. Consequently a further curtailment of purchasing power and a further diversion of labour to war purposes has become an essential part of our war financing programme.
It will be recollected that last year I criticized the minister's budget on the ground that it had not faced, with sufficient realism, the problem of consumer spending. The enormous increase in retail sales during the last year has demonstrated that I was justified in that criticism, and I am glad to note now that, not only in his income tax proposals but in his new taxation of luxury commodities, the minister has met, in a measure at least- perhaps to a large degree-the criticism which I offered last year.
I now turn to the minister's second objective, which was, of course, the raising of additional revenue. He estimates that the increased yield from the personal income tax will be 45 millions of dollars for the remainder of the present fiscal year, and 115 millions of dollars for a full year. That is a large increase, and I do not believe that people will visualize just how large it is unless a comparison is made with what they have been paying heretofore under the same heading.
The magnitude of this increase is perhaps best illustrated by the fact that in the fiscal year 1938-39 the total personal income tax collections amounted to only 46 millions of dollars. In the fiscal year 1939-40. during seven months of which we were at war, the total income tax collections amounted to only 45 millions of dollars. In other words, the total increased yield from the tax increases for the remainder of the present fiscal year is as much as our total collections from personal income tax in the fiscal year 1939-40, during seven months of which we were at war. Our total income tax collections, including national defence tax, for the first full fiscal year during which we were at war, namely 1940-41, amounted to only 106 millions of dollars. Consequently the anticipated yield from the increased rates for a full year is almost 10 millions of dollars more than our total

These three, then, were the objectives which the minister had in view in presenting his proposals, and the success of his proposals must be judged largely by the manner in which they attain the objectives.
In addition to stating his proposals, the minister laid down three standards or criteria on the basis of which to judge his proposals- 44561-240 J
namely the need for equity, for incentive, and for savings. That these are proper criteria I would not disagree; I think perhaps we all agree, although we may not be completely in accord on the question whether the minister's proposals are fully in line with all these criteria.
The minister mentioned the danger that high progressive rates of income tax may interfere with the incentive for harder and better work for efficient production; and well he may. There is such a thing as killing the goose that lays the golden egg. In mentioning this the minister recognized, of course, the important role which profit plays in the life of every individual, every last one of us. I would hope that the proposals have not too seriously interfered with that instinctive craving of individual human beings, and that the people of this country will respond to the urgent necessity of making service to the state-let me emphasize that-in this time of national crisis their major incentive to greater and more efficient production. Service to the state, not private profit or private gain, should be the standard for every one of us.
I propose to turn now to a discussion of some of the highlights of the proposals themselves. I think it is only on the anvil of discussion we can get to understand these proposals. That is one of my excuses, not an apology, for occupying the time of this house on this very hot afternoon, and if I add something to the sum total of the knowledge of hon. members I am sure they will forgive me.
The first important change is what the minister speaks of as the combination of the national defence tax and the graduated income tax into a single assessment. In committee we shall be able to analyse these imposts and determine whether the minister has gone far enough in the combination of the two taxes. What is now spoken of as the "normal" rate of tax appears in reality to be substantially the old national defence tax. It differs in principle from the graduated income tax in that is is assessable against the total income of any person whose income exceeds certain specified amounts. In view of the attempt which will be made to deduct both types of income tax at the source, I hope the minister will explain to the committee why he has not made a full and complete combination of the two taxes into a single graduated tax-in other words, added the percentages required to be paid under the normal tax to the percentages required to be paid under the graduated income tax, properly adjusted to produce the same revenue. This would have meant greater simplicity, I submit, both for
3792	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
the individual taxpayer and for the tax officials of the Department of National Revenue. There may be good reasons why this was not done, but I should like the minister to explain fully in. the committee stage just why it was not done. T have a shrewd suspicion as to what the reason was. By this method of putting the normal taxon the full amount of taxable income the minister desires to draw a larger sum from the lower wage and lower salaried people than he would by a complete combination. 1 think that is incontrovertible.
I am bound to say that I think the increase in rates of the normal tax as opposed to the old national defence tax was expected. I do not think there will be great objection. I believe it will make for equality of sacrifice, a principle for which I have always contended. The increase, however, in the graduated taxes is tremendously heavy, although, as the minister pointed out, there are certain alleviating features which are introduced into our financial system for the first time, and which I shall discuss a little later. These increases will bear heavily upon all classes of our citizenship and will involve a very substantial change in the mode of living of practically every class of our Canadian people. Subject to certain inequalities which I shall point out later, and which I hope the minister will undertake to rectify, I believe the Canadian people will assume this burden in the same spirit of patriotism and willingness to sacrifice as [DOT] they have assumed every other burden which they have been called1 upon to bear since the outbreak of the war. These increases are part of the price which we must pay for victory. I do not believe there is any class of our Canadian citizenry who are not prepared to place their last dollar at the government's disposal if it will mean the triumph of our institutions over the forces of evil and terror.
The next important feature in the income tax resolutions is the proposal to collect payments by regular deduction at the source, or, where that is impracticable, by compulsory instalment payment. There will be objections to this procedure in some quarters. There are many deductions from pay envelopes now. There is grumbling, and demands will be made for higher and higher salaries and wages to meet these deductions. In the early stages of the war these demands were met by many employers. This new deduction will cause a good deal of irritation; but, having considered the matter from every angle, I do not intend to oppose the procedure. I realize that this is the easiest method by which the government can get the money,

and this is the surest method by which payments will be made. It must be obvious, I think, to all of us that the tax rates have reached such a level that their payment must be a matter of grave anxiety to the taxpayer and a matter of monthly budgeting by every one of us.
I was rather disappointed to hear the minister say in the course of his speech that only a minority had availed themselves of the heretofore existing voluntary instalment plan. I believe that plan was both good and useful, I used it myself. I was compelled to use it, and I found it satisfactory. The new plan of deduction at the source, or the compulsory instalment payment, will bring not only increased revenue but earlier revenue to the treasury, and it will above everything else help to curb consumer-spending by preventing prodigal and spendthrift individuals from going on a buying spree, thus utilizing unnecessary consumer goods and then finding themselves unable to meet their obligations to the state.
The minister has changed the whole principle of exemptions m respect of dependency. Instead of allowing specific sums as exemptions in respect of marriage and dependents, the minister proposes in effect to freeze the value of exemptions at the amount which they have been worth under existing tax rates, to a taxpayer with an income of between $2,500 and $3,000. This feature of the minister's proposal is open to serious objection, and in my view works unwarranted hardship upon the family man as opposed to the single person. I am sure the minister will agree that the family man should be in no less favourable position than the single man or woman, but that is exactly what is occurring and that is where he is being put. He is being put in a less favourable position.
No matter what the economic status of a husband may be, he will now be allowed only $150 deduction in respect of his wife and $S0 in respect of each child. Surely no one will suggest that there is any equity in this. Surely no one will assert that the obligations of a married man with two children are only S310 per annum greater than those of a single person. Surely no one will suggest that the obligations of a married man who must buy or rent quarters and provide clothing and food for his family, must- provide for the education of his children and the security of his dependents in the event of anything happening to him, are so little greater than those of a single person. Is it right that a man with the responsibilities of a home should be given only $150 per anum consideration for having undertaken those responsibilities, and

The Budget-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
an additional S80 for each child whom he maintains? I ask the minister to reconsider that whole position. It is not fair; it is not just.
The minister stated that other changes would have the effect of widening the differences between single and married persons and those with children. While some of the changes do perhaps have this result in an indirect way, I do not believe that any of them are of such a nature that they will place persons of these different marital circumstances upon a substantial equilibrium. I give the minister and the house an example of what I consider to be a glaring case of discrimination and inequity. A single man earning 13,000 a year will contribute total taxes and compulsory savings amounting to $1,064 per annum; a married man with two children, with all the responsibilities of a home, education and all that goes with the maintenance of a family of four, earning $3,000 a year, will contribute total taxes and compulsory savings amounting to S668 per annum. The single man will thus be left with $1,936 net income per annum, while the married man with two children will be left with $2,332 per annum, or less than $400 more than the single man. Is it right that the man with the responsibilities of a home should be allowed less than $400 per annum consideration for having undertaken those responsibilities? I believe the old system was much more equitable and just. It recognized the undoubted fact that as a man's income status becomes higher his necessary family obligations increase, and so his tax exemptions operated to decrease proportionately his tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But were not those nearer together in the past?

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
These are my deductions. The minister can analyse them any way he likes. I think I am right.
The old system recognized that an attempt should be made to achieve a comparative equity between married and single persons. Now all that is gone by the board and the family life of this nation will inevitably suffer.
I draw this particularly to the attention of the house and particularly of the Prime Minister. I hope he will give some consideration to this question. It is the only appeal I shall make to him in regard to the matter of taxation. Heretofore my observation has been that he has never paid much attention to these questions of taxation. I fail to recall in recent years any occasion on which he has intervened in the budget debate or expressed any opinion on fiscal policy.
I want to point out, and I draw this particularly to the minister's attention, that the object of his fiscal policy, an object with
which I agree, is to reduce inflationary spending on useless commodities and services. It is notorious that our young single citizens are the chief contributors to the wave of useless and wasteful purchasing of non-essential goods and services which is a fundamental cause of inflationary danger.
Do not let it be said that I am arguing the case of the rich man. Nothing is further from my intention. I am arguing the case of the small and medium earning class who have undertaken responsibilities to the nation and who should not be penalized but should be given encouragement to fulfil them. Those who say that to retain the old system would help the rich man do not appreciate the fact that the maximum exemption which could possibly be allowed under the old system would be, in the case of a man with an income of $500,000, only 98 per cent of $750-not a very substantial sum for a man with an income of $500,000. If it is thought that to retain the old system, would assist the wealthy man too much, then I suggest that the old system be adopted up to a specified ceiling and that the exemption should not then operate at any higher rate. The man I am tiying to help is the man of small and moderate income, and I believe that this change works upon the married man of that class a most unfair discrimination.
I consider this proposal a retrograde step, and I urge the minister to revert to the old system, which was much more just and equitable than his new proposal. The youth of any nation is its greatest asset. Anything which tends to discourage the raising of a family is a vital and oppressive blow to the future of any nation, and this proposal does just that. People cannot afford to have children. If Canada is to be a great nation in the future she must have greater population, and the most satisfactory way to achieve an increase in population is to encourage the raising of children steeped in Canadian tradition rather than through immigration of persons steeped in the traditions of other lands. I therefore urge most strongly upon the minister the reconsideration of this proposal, and I sincerely hope he will change it.
As a measure of alleviation of the steep increase in income tax, the minister has proposed the adoption of three new principles:
1.	Exemption of medical and hospital expenses in excess of 5 per cent of income;
2.	Establishing a proportion of the tax as a minimum savings requirement, which will be held to the credit of the taxpayer as a refundable credit, with accrued interest at 2 per cent;
3.	Deduction from the minimum savings requirements of amounts paid in respect of superannuation, life insurance, and principal payments on mortgages on homes.
3794	COMMONS
The Budget

Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
So far as the first principle is concerned, I am sure that every member of his house, especially those who belong to the medical profession, will be in agreement. Indeed so far as I am concerned I would hope that this might be a permanent feature of the income tax structure. When the tragedy of serious illness befalls a family, the drain on the family income is frequently such that for the state to tax the amounts spent constitutes a most serious hardship. It occurs to me that perhaps the principle will require to be broadened somewhat. As it now stands it does not appear to cover those not unusual cases where the actual expenditure for a physician or for hospitalization is not large, but where the expenses of the individual for medicines prescribed by the physician reach very large sums. I have in mind as an example those who are required to use insulin. I hope the minister in committee will see fit to broaden the resolution to include such cases, although I appreciate that there might be great difficulty in doing so, and perhaps some danger.
Earlier I mentioned, in passing, the new principle of minimum savings requirement, which has been largely adopted from the deferred pay theory of Lord Keynes. I mentioned also that this is a principle which has been advocated from time to time by members on this side of the house. I am glad to see that the minister has adopted the principle. This minimum savings requirement, as part of the general increase in the tax rate, strikes at the problem of unnecessary consumption of consumer goods. The provision for the return of the specified sums in the post-war period means that the individual now forgoes or postpones consumption in order that he may enjoy it at a later period when that consumption will be more advantageous to the economic good of the nation. This plan of deferring or postponing consumption will be, I hope, an important feature in post-war recovery. The release to individual taxpayers after the war of the sums which they will now establish to their credit will lead to a demand for consumer goods after the war and will thereby help to start the wheels of the ordinary economic system in renewed and vigorous operation. Therefore I believe the principle to be a sound one, not only for the present but for the future. There are a number of matters in connection with the practical application of the theory which will require to be clarified when the house is in committee, but I commend the principle itself.
I should like at this stage to reiterate what the minister emphasized in his budget speech, namely, that the refundable portion of the tax is merely a minimum savings requirement.

It does not absolve the taxpayer from the patriotic obligation of contributing to his utmost to voluntary savings methods. It is obvious from the minister's speech that new taxation alone will not begin to meet the financial requirements of this country, and that hitherto unheard-of sums will have to be raised by direct borrowing from the people. I have sufficient confidence in the Canadian people, as the minister himself has expressed, to believe that they will respond to their patriotic duty and will endeavour to save, over and above the amounts which they will be called upon to contribute as minimum savings requirements, as much as it is possible for them to do, and will invest it in war savings certificates and victory loans. To do so will require rigorous and plain and simple living on the part of every one of us. I am prepared to make that sacrifice. So are we all, I believe.
An important feature of the minimum savings requirement is the third principle to which I alluded, namely, the deduction from the minimum savings requirement of amounts paid in respect of superannuation, insurance, and principal on mortgages. In other words, credit is being given to the frugal individual who has taken his own means to provide for his own future. The minister has recognized that such a person should not be required to contribute twice and, in addition, that such payments are not of an inflationary character.
Another type of payment for which I believe provision should be made is that under agreements for sale. Such payments are identical in principle with principal payments on a mortgage, and I hope the minister will see fit to include them.
The minister's proposal, as it now stands, will rectify what has always seemed to me to be an inequality. In the past a person contributing to an organized pension or superannuation deduction scheme was entitled to claim exemptions in respect of his payments, whereas the individual who had not the benefit of such a scheme, but who must provide the equivalent by the purchase of government annuities or life insurance as a means of securing himself for the future, was not permitted any deduction. I am glad to see that this inequality has been done away with.
There is just one other feature of this vast increase in personal income tax to which I desire to allude. I call the minister's attention to it particularly. It must be recognized that personal income is of two classes, namely, that earned by the personal effort of the taxpayer, and that received from investments either accumulated or acquired by inheritance. The taxpayer in the fortunate position of owning investments can obviously meet a

The Budget-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
difficult situation by selling some of his investments. On the other hand, the taxpayer whose income is derived in the main from personal earnings-say a lawyer, a doctor, or one receiving a salary-has no such happy recourse.
Events of recent years have left many people with debts that they are honestly and valiantly struggling to pay off. The new taxes take such a toll of their earnings that in many cases there will be little or nothing left to apply on old debts. It is surely in the public interest that debtors be given reasonable encouragement to pay their debts. Under conditions now envisaged, this will become practically impossible. It would be only fair and equitable if the government would permit an exemption, with respect to earned income, to the extent of, say, 10 per cent to enable the taxpayer to pay debts contracted before the war. In the aggregate the amount could not be important in relation to the total income tax. But it would in very many cases encourage and assist honest people to pay their old debts, and thereby help to maintain their morale and their feeling that there is something left to work for. People of this type should not be driven to the bankruptcy courts.
I do suggest to the minister that some provision must be made for people in the circumstances to which I have alluded, and I believe an exemption of the type which I have mentioned would serve the purpose best.
I wish to refer now to the excess profits tax. These are important business taxes. Important principles are involved.
In the first war session of September, 1939, we witnessed the introduction and, a few months later, the abandonment of a hastily drawn and ill-conceived excess profits tax. It never was put in operation. It had many inherent defects. I shall not enter into a discussion of these, but it laid down the principle that excess profits over normal or basic profits would be subject to special taxation and so make available to the state a substantial portion of the excess profits made. Its enactment in eighteen hours was hailed as a demonstration that democracy could act with speed on occasion. The present act is based on the statute of 1940.
We on the opposition side of this house have never opposed or criticized the principle of taxation of excess profits. We have all, I think, subscribed to the principle that no one shall become rich out of the war. Whatever criticism has been offered has arisen from the incidence of the tax and its application. That is a fair and legitimate subject of examination and criticism. In my opinion, due regard was
not had, up to this budget, to the plight of many industrial corporations which, during the ten-year period of the depression, 19291939, had a hectic time to keep alive, not to speak of their obligations to their employees and to the communities which they served and in which they functioned. An attempt was made-which I believe in a measure has been successful, although only partly so-to classify those who were in the so-called "depressed industry" category. I have always thought this effort was praiseworthy and I believe the system established was fairly satisfactory. A board of referees was set up, composed of men of high calibre and good character, men who went about their work conscientiously. But I do not believe and never have believed that the base was broad enough.
There is a feature of our excess profits taxation on corporations and individual proprietors to which I desire to direct attention. Last year I asked the house and the country this question: If you continue to exact high corporation income and excess profits taxes, and still higher personal income taxes-and I agree that we must do so if we are to continue to pay as much as possible of our war costs out of current revenue

if you continue to exact huge so-called excess profits from these same sources, how will these individual proprietors and companies be in a position to meet the exacting post-war period of transition and change from a war-time economy to peacetime activity?
In particular, I then asked what thought have those master minds, who behind the scenes are formulating our war-time financial policies, given to the problem of enabling these same companies to provide the employment for our returned soldiers and our civilian population which it is so necessary to provide if we are to escape that dread period of unemployment which will inevitably descend upon us within a measurable period of time after the close of hostilities? These men have responsibilities; they have great power; but they are not answerable to anybody. I put this question to them-and they will probably all disappear and get out from under by the time the post-war period arrives.

speechtext:
I dare say the minister will, but I suggest that it is to these gentlemen I wish to speak, these men who are formulating the fiscal policy of Canada, men with great power and no responsibility.
3796	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Hanson (Y'ork-Sunbury)
I then asserted that that situation must be faced. I have asserted with assurance on more than one occasion, both here and elsewhere, that no matter how wise government planning may be, no matter how much, you may continue with economic controls, no matter what plans may be laid, nothing can ever effectively be1 substituted for the principle of private employment, which is based on the broader principle of private enterprise.
I believe that unless you keep these private enterprises strong and healthy-supervised and controlled, if you will, wisely and effectively- you will have no cushion upon which these industrial undertakings can rest during that trying period which, plan as we will, is bound to come. Unless they have adequate reserves to fall back upon, then the old problem of unemployment will be upon our backs, as it was in the days following the last war and in the long dreary days which preceded this war The answer to my appeal, the reasonableness of which no one will deny, is found in that portion of the budget proposals which deals with this subject. The minister takes the ground that the act of 1940, by which certain basic and excess profits taxes were imposed, was appropriate to the period of expansion during the early stages of the war. Undoubtedly it has produced a substantial amount of revenue, but I doubt that it has always been reasonably equitable. However, I have no time to debate that point now. The minister now states that the time has come when we can and should make the tax more severe, and he proposes now to take the full 100 per cent . instead of 75 per cent, but with a compensating feature. Personally I would prefer another method, but I shall not argue the point now. i He proposes to increase the rate of tax on * excess profits but not the flat rate of tax which applies to profits generally. I agree with the latter point of view, for obvious reasons. But I wonder if he is correct in his hypothesis that, in taking 100 per cent excess profits, he will not be removing the incentive for economy and efficiency in production. I hope he is , right, but human nature being what it is, I may be at least pardoned if I am sceptical.
By taking the full 100 per cent, even though he leaves the flat rate of tax alone, he is in a degree depriving business of the right and duty to build up reserves-adequate reserves-for the post-war period. As a counter-balance, however, the minister proposes that, after having raised the rate from 75 per cent to 100 per cent, provision will be made-subject, as I understand it, to certain limitations-for refunding after the war, presumably after the ; official cessation of hostilities, to the taxpayer who has paid the 100 per cent rate on excess 
profits, 20 per cent of the amount of profits in excess of the amount at which the 100 per cent tax on the excess after the deduction of corporation income tax and the 12 per cent flat rate equals the 10 per cent tax on the total profit. This is a very obscure provision. Clearly it requires further clarification and elucidation. It is complicated, and I admit that I do not fully comprehend it. For this I may be pardoned. I wonder how many hon. members of this house comprehend it? I WQnder how many members of the government who gave assent to this budget know what this means? I do not think any one of them outside the minister knows what it means. I suggest that the 20 per cent refund applies only when the 100 per cent rate effectively applies on any additional profits. This is a great limitation. It does not mean exactly a refund of 20 per cent of excess profits where the effective rate is paid, but only after certain other factors are computed. I invite the minister to clarify the position in the committee stage. The sum to be returned is without interest, but is unconditional except as to liability to the crown for any unpaid tax accrued.

speechtext: That is a nice touch.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The outstanding principle is clear. These companies will have allocated to them on the books of the nation credits varying in amounts for the express purpose of enabling them to function in giving employment in the trying post-war period. This idea is not original with this government. I have hardly found any original idea in any budget. They have all been copied from something and made to apply to conditions in Canada. Some such a scheme has been established in Britain, although there are differences in the details and different limitations. When there in September last I had a long and most interesting interview with the chancellor of the exchequer, Sir Kingsley Wood, and I discussed this very matter with him.
They have no corporation income tax in Britain, but they have an excess profits tax of 100 per cent over and above standard profits. I have often thought that system would have been the proper one for Canada and preferable to our present system. It avoids the reproach of double or even treble taxation. This reproach has been levelled across the floor of the house on many occasions. I remember well that when the then hon. member for Waterloo North was the Minister of National Revenue I levelled criticism at the proposals made in the 1920's, and he admitted that the charge was well founded. It is probable that

The Budget-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
it is too late now to change our system, but it was quite possible to have done so in 1939 and 1940, when the corporation income tax could have been vacated, the income taxed in the hands of the shareholders, and an excess profits tax of 100 per cent established from the very beginning. Business men, I believe, would have accepted it; in fact, those with whom I discussed the problem favoured it.
This was not done. It showed, in my view, a lack of vision, a lack of the realities of the situation which will confront us in the days to come. But because we have the present system fastened upon us, it is still, in my opinion, necessary and quite feasible to prepare for the post-war period by setting up, on the nation s books, credits for those who are paying so much in taxation so that they may-under government control, if you will-be able to function normally in the post-war period and provide that measure of employment and contentment which only private enterprise can provide. I approve the principle, even if I do not clearly understand the details. It is enough if I enunciate the principle which I think should guide us.. It has been studied with great care by the treasury officials in Britain. They have no doubt of its soundness and of its necessity. I had intended to offer it as a constructive suggestion to the minister and to the gentlemen, from the head of the Bank of Canada down, who are advising him.
The minister indicated that other and minor amendments to the act will be brought down. I shall only allude to one-that relating to small business. I refer principally to owner-managed businesses. These men are in many cases facing ruin as a result of present taxation and cbntrols. At present the law gives complete exemption to small businesses with profits of $5,000 or less. The minister states that this exemption in respect of the new 12 per cent flat rate will be withdrawn. If this means that taxation is to be made greater and heavier for them, I regret it; for under present conditions of price ceilings and similar restrictions, their plight is a difficult one.
On the whole, I congratulate the Minister of Finance on his action in providing that these taxpayers may recover, even in somewhat limited circumstances, 20 per cent of the 100 per cent excess profits tax at the close of the war, for the purpose of permitting the modernization, reconstruction, or readaptation of their factories, and, much more important, for providing working capital and employment which will then be so necessary.
I just want to say a word to the socialist party in this house in regard to this proposal. They will probably criticize the minister for
making what they will allege to be a concession to the profit motive and to capitalism. My own feeling is that fundamentally it is a concession to the very important purpose of permitting employers to find jobs for their workers. I should like to take this opportunity to say to our socialist friends that they are never going to become the true representatives of the Canadian worker until they realize that the one point on which the Canadian worker does approve capitalism is as an employer furnishing jobs-not talking about employment, but furnishing jobs. The Canadian working man knows his common interest with his employer on this point, however much he may differ with him on the details of how the jobs are to be furnished.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are not arguing that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are the only ones speaking on behalf of labour?

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Certainly not. In other words, the Canadian worker has a pride in his employer's success, provided that the employer passes on to him the employment, under proper working conditions, that is so necessary for his own well-being and happiness. If you want an instance of that, look at the two great railway systems in this country and how loyal the workmen are to their employers. I doubt whether any socialist speaks for the railway workers of this country.
I have one last word to say to the socialist party on this point. When the socialist party tries to criticize the minister's action in this respect, I should like to remind them that a great English labour leader, Sir Walter Citrine, told the Canadian club in Montreal not a year ago that English labour was tired of being misrepresented to the public by politicians and college professors.
I want to say a word with respect to the succession duty. I am glad to note that the minister has yielded to the theory that charitable gifts shall be entirely free of duty. If I recollect aright, I urged this course a ' year ago. The experience of a few months must have indicated to him that it was a mistake to impose even one-half the ordinary rate on such gifts. The reason is obvious. No matter how well intentioned a person having property to dispose of, by will or otherwise, may be, he instinctively feels that if the state steps in and confiscates twice, perhaps thrice, a portion of his capital assets, the state thereby releases him from obligations which, under different circumstances, he himself would assume. If the state takes that which under ordinary circumstances would go to charities,
3798	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
then the state itself must assume those responsibilities. As a result of two, sometimes three, capital levies on the same dollar, plus high taxation for war, and levies for war purposes, charitable gifts have been rapidly receding. I congratulate the minister upon having seen the light, and changed his tune.
Now a word on indirect taxes. The minister has made another of his selective approaches to indirect taxation. He recommends substantial increases in taxes which fall on luxury expenditures. With the general principle involved I am in agreement. Any reasonable measure which will prevent or discourage such expenditures merits support. The money is required for other purposes.
With regard to the excise duties on alcoholic beverages, his approach is definitely not that of restricting consumption, but rather of securing additional revenue. It is of no use to tell this house that $2 a gallon added to the excise duty on spirits will reduce sales and expenditures. The only effect will be to raise the retail prices on domestic whisky from present levels by a small amount. Already I believe the Ontario liquor commission has announced new prices-25 cents more here, 35 cents there, with a maximum of 75 cents on a large quart. Does anyone mean to tell me that any person in Canada who wants a bottle of whisky will stop at the additional impost? The idea is ridiculous. Let any member of this house who uses liquor as a beverage pause and ask himself if he will refrain from buying a bottle of whisky because the government has raised the excise duty by $2 a gallon. The answer is obvious.
I do not know what the effect of the increase on malt will be on the price of beer. I should think not much-15 cents per dozen bottles, perhaps. I have heard that former increases did not perceptibly increase prices. I understood that the brewers, generally speaking, absorbed the increases. Certainly those two increases had no effect on the quantity purchased by the public. On the contrary, sales have steadily increased, I venture to predict that this increase from 12 to 16 cents on malt will not divert any dollars from consumer expenditure. This whole situation, Mr. Speaker, has given cause for grave anxiety in Canada. I fear that the drinking habit is increasing in this country. The drink bill in Canada has increased from $153 million in 1938 to $232 million in 1940, an increase of almost $80 million in two years, and I am told that this year's drink bill will probably reach as high a figure as $290 million. Recently representations have been made to the Prime Minister with regard to this matter. The liquor trade is a thriving trade, and it is the

only trade known to me over which control has not been exercised, except by way of taxation.
Recently the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) quoted1 in this house an extract from the "Brewers' Magazine", from which I shall quote two sentences:
One of the finest things that could have happened the brewing industry was the insistence of high ranking officers-
'Meaning high ranking officers in the army, I assume:
-to make beer available at army camps.
Then mark this. It goes on:
Here is a chance for brewers to cultivate a taste for beer in millions of young men who will eventually constitute the largest beerconsuming section of our population.
I confess, Mr. Speaker, that when I heard that I was appalled at the implications. The whole general effect will be more revenue from all these sources, and the alleged objective will not be attained. There is only one way to deal with this problem-for problem it is-and that is to make it impossible to expend such vast sums of money on alcoholic and malt beverages; and that apparently is the last thing in the world this government- or the provincial governments either, for that matter-wish to do. They know that the tremendous drink bill of this country is a serious drain on the people of Canada of money which should be diverted to other and better purposes, but neither authority will deal with it.
I shall not refer to the new taxes on cigarettes, smoking tobacco, cigars, and the like. I doubt if the new imposts will cut down consumption. They may. Meanwhile we are to receive in excess of fifteen millions of dollars of new revenue from the one source, and twenty-three millions of dollars from the other-and I suspect that is really what the minister is after.
I wish to refer to the tax on candy. This undoubtedly is imposed on the theory that candy is a luxury. I dispute that premise absolutely. Candy is an important food. It is probably the best energizing food, particularly for young people, because of its sugar and cocoa content. Our soldiers on active service use it for emergency rations. Our Atlantic pilots carry it on their trips, and I believe the commando troops take it with them as emergency rations. Recently Mr. Morgenthau recommended a 15 per cent tax on candy in his message to congress, and the committee threw it out, because candy is such an important food and uses many farm products-butter, milk, cream, et cetera.

The Budget-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
Candy is the only food which is taxed in this budget. Cheap jewellery is exempt from $1 down, but a tax is put on the candy sold to children. This is not just figurative, because it will actually be done. All penny goods will have to be eliminated; a child with six cents can buy a chocolate bar, but a child with one or two cents cannot buy anything.
There is another aspect of this matter which should be considered. With the restriction on sugar, children will get less sugar and now they will also get less candy. It will be bound to have a detrimental effect on the health of the rising generation. I say to the minister that this tax is unnecessary, and he ought not to pursue it.
Time will not permit me to make reference to the large number of other taxes, generally described as "nuisance taxes". We had them in the last war. I suppose we shall have to submit to them, as we did then. The only excuse for most of them is that the country needs the money. On that theory they will be accepted, but on the distinct understanding that we shall be rid of them at the earliest possible moment. I fear that, is a vain hope. Never again shall we be able to face life freed from the major part of these small, petty, nuisance imposts.
There is one redeeming feature, and it is this. The people of this country, who have become soft and prodigal in their personal spending in normal times, will once again have to scrimp and adopt the old-fashioned virtue of thrift-one of the real virtues, one which our parents practised, one which they endeavoured to instil into us as children, but which, alas! most of us in the easy days of the 1920's soon forgot and failed to practise. It will come back to us. It is being forced upon us, and it will be a good thing for us and for our children. It will teach us and them the principles of self-denial. That, at least, will be worth while.
I have either read or listened to all the budgets which have been delivered in this house for the past forty years. Even in peace time none of them are all good or all bad; but in peace time it is easy to criticize, easy to suggest that some other fiscal policy, some other tax, some other proposal, should be adopted. Per contra, it is usually easy to support some of the proposals in any peace time budget.
One of the difficulties which confronts me, and which always confronts one in my position at any time, is that one is obliged, on a motion to go into committee of ways and means, either to accept the budget outright or wholly to reject it. But the difficulties are
greatly accentuated when one is dealing with a war budget, a budget of such dimensions as almost to stagger one with its enormous figures and implications.
It has not been difficult to criticize the budget in its details, to find fault with this feature and that, to say that, from one point of view, it is soaking the rich; and from another angle there is concealed in this budget power to exact an undue portion of the national revenue from the wage-earners of this country-and there is substantial truth in the latter statement.
But having heard this budget delivered at the darkest hour in the history of this war, when the situation is more critical than at any time since Dunkirk; having since read1 it with care, and endeavoured to master the huge mass of figures and the underlying principles, realizing as I do that we are passing through a world revolution, a very convulsion of civilization itself, I have come to the conclusion that the proper and patriotic course for me is to support the general budget proposals. My reason, my convictions, tell me that we must raise this huge sum of money, by some means or other, and to argue at this time that some . other ways or means are preferable has no great appeal to me.
And let us not hear anything more of failure to conscript wealth. We are conscripting wealth. We had it in the 1941 budget, notwithstanding what some people may say or think. We have had it since 1940. We have it here, in stark reality. Also, those who are not possessed of accumulated wealth, those whose wealth consists of their week-to-week and mouth-to-mouth wages, those who are in receipt of the major part of the increased national income-their wealth is being conscripted by this budget too. They are paying-paying much more than appears from the skilfully disguised language employed by the minister. They will be called upon to pay the major part of the new millions which the minister hopes to get under the new personal income and other tax rates. The method or manner of approach to them is skilfully concealed and not so brutal as to those in the higher brackets. It is hidden in a mass of verbiage, but the power to withhold from the pay cheques of the wage earners and the lower salaried classes the greater part of these new levies is embodied in these resolutions, and they will pay by far the heaviest portion of these new imposts.
I point out as a matter of information, and information only, the following facts:
1. Up to this budget, the group earning over $2,000 per annum were 58 per cent of the
3800	COMMONS

Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
income taxpayers, and they paid 97 per cent of the amount paid in personal income taxes. They have been called upon to make great sacrifices, but there has been no great complaint from them.
2.	The group under 82,000 constituted 42 per cent of the taxpayers, and they paid 3 per cent -of the tax collected.
3.	Under the present proposals, based on the status of a married man with two children, the tax on an income of 81,250 has now been increased 45-1 per cent; on one with an income of $2,000, 258 per cent; and on 83,000, 211 per cent.
4.	Then the curve of increased taxation is reversed. On $5,000, the increase is 126 per cent; on $10,000, 68 per cent; and on 850,000, 30 per cent.
The undoubted fact is that those in the lower group of $3,000 and under are being subjected to a very sudden and steep levy.
But let us not flinch from -our obligations. Let us face the situation with courage and fortitude. Let us make every sacrifice. We are all together in this great adventure. There are no favoured few. Together we shall either survive or go under. Let us resolve that survive we shall.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) has completely excelled himself this afternoon-. I cannot recall having heard him deliver a speech more thoughtfully prepared, or more meaty, or more genuinely valuable. It was devoid of all forms of bitterness and party animus, and altogether it was a fine effort. I wish to congratulate him on it. . But I do not wish to leave the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) entirely without commendation. As I have said on more than one occasion, he is the man who has the greatest burden in Canada to-day, and his task is made more difficult by the fact that he is endeavouring to carry on in a power age with an ox-cart financial system. That is almost tantamount to a man's undertaking to equip an army with bows and arrows in order to meet tanks. The mere fact that the minister is endeavouring to cariy on under that handicap is cause for congratulating him even more sincerely than one would under ordinary circumstances.
With respect to the budget, I do not desire to be in any wray unkindly or harshly critical.
I should have been pleased if upon this occasion I could have had my speech carefully written out weeks beforehand so that I could read it, but the rules of the house

deny me any such privilege. I must therefore do my best to clothe my thoughts in language as I stand here facing a critical situation.
The attitude to budgets is changing rather rapidly, I fancy, in the world. There was a time when a budget was looked upon simply as a means of raising money, but to-day the budget is regarded as much more than that. It must be a means of regulating the whole economy of a country. To illustrate the truthfulness of what I have said, and to indicate that in this statement I am in reasonably good company, may I read from "Fiscal Policy and Business Cycles", a book copyrighted by Alvin H. Hanson, of Harvard university in 1941. I quote from page 187:
For the public economy expenditures ought to be weighed not in terms of the profit and loss of the state itself but rather in terms of the effect of such expenditures ou the full and efficient functioning of the economy as a whole. Fiscal policy is an important instrument for maximizing the real income of a community and for regulating the distribution of income and wealth.
As I deal with this budget I shall have in mind more particularly the assertion which is made in -the second sentence. I read that statement from page 187 in the chapter "budgetary theory -and practice". In the first place, I wish to make two or three comments on the budget itself and on the inconsistencies which arise from the difficulty of the minister's position rather than from any inadequacy or inefficiency on his part.
The budget lacks unity because it aims at two things. It has two objectives. The first is to raise money, and the second is to withdraw from the' people purchasing power, thereby relieving buying pressure upon prices and tending to offset the tendency to inflation. Since the minister is aiming at two objects all the time he cannot -be blamed for forgetting one of them once in a while and being really at a loss to know which object he is pursuing at any given moment. As I listened to him, I thought he hardly knew, in the case of any given impost, whether he had in mind chiefly the raising of money or the withdrawal of purchasing power. As a matter of fact, theoretically, the principle of withdrawing purchasing power should be his principal object, and not the raising of money. He would very much dislike to acknowledge that,
I fancy, and I know many good gentlemen, prominent in Canadian financial affairs, who would dread to acknowledge it. But it is unfortunately true, and that is one of the momentous facts predicable of our time, that the object of a budget is no longer to raise money but to withdraw .purchasing power.

The Budget-Mr. Blachmore
If we could once grant that the whole object of this budget had been the withdrawal of purchasing power, the incidence of these taxes would have been placed in an altogether different position as regards many imposts.
Is this budget as it stands designed primarily to raise money or to guard against inflation? If it is designed to guard against inflation, to prevent people from buying the things they desire to buy, did the minister have in mind the object of preventing the people from buying life insurance? If he had not in mind preventing people from buying life insurance, why would he withdraw purchasing power until they were unable to buy life insurance? Yet this compromising position has been thrust upon the minister and his department. Did he wish to prevent people from repaying debts? The repayment of a debt would hardly cause inflation, for in most cases the money would go immediately to the bank and the money used in payment of the debt would be dead for that cycle. Did he wish to prevent them from having dental care, or from having medical treatment, or from sending letters by paying postal rates, or from buying flowers and shrubs to decorate and beautify their homes, or from buying breeding stock such as cattle, horses, sheep, swine, poultry, bees and the like, to increase their productive capacity? Did he wish to prevent them from buying fences or building fences, or from getting timber to make fence posts with which to build fences? By these imposts he has successfully contrived to prevent them from buying a good many such things, the purchase of hardly any one of which would tend to cause inflation. I think I have said enough about the inconsistency of the budget, an inconsistency which results from the difficulty of the minister's position and not from his inefficiency or inadequacy in any respect.
Again, the budget is inequitable. I am not saying that the minister did not do what he considered his very best in an endeavour to make it equitable. He said specifically in his speech that in framing the budget his object was to recognize the need of equity, incentive and saving. That indicated a fine power of discernment in the minister, a fine appreciation of values. But in my opinion he has fallen far short of providing equity and incentive in many cases. As the leader of the opposition pointed out very well, I thought, sufficient to render it unnecessary for me to repeat except by reference, this budget bears destructively upon the less well-to-do among Canadians.
The sales tax-I hardly recall whether or not the leader of the opposition mentioned it -is designed to raise $218,000,000 in 1942. A
disproportionate amount of that will be taken from the less prosperous. The people who are straining every nerve and lying awake nights trying to make ends meet are being bled of their substance in a dozen and one different ways of which they are not really aware, by an 8 per cent sales tax stealing in upon them and completely unavoidable. While that impost was not levied in this budget, yet it was continued in this budget. I believe that the time has come for the removal of a large part of the sales tax, if not all of it.
The minister has borne with harsh insistence upon those with incomes of $3,000 a year and under. The leader of the opposition in his closing remarks referred to an article in the June 27 number of the Financial Post, a portion of which I shall read:
The tax on an income of $1,250 lias now been increased 45'5 per cent. On $2,000 income the increase is 258 per cent. On $3,000 it is 211 per cent. There comes the dividing line. For incomes above that figure the percentage increase declines. At .$5,000 the increase is 126 per cent; at $10,000 it is 08 per cent, and at $50,000 it is a 30 per cent increase.
I rarely mention personal matters in this house, but when I was elected to parliament I had nine children. My income would have come in that $1,250 bracket and would have been subject to that increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Surely not. You get $80
exemption for a child.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, provided there
are the children, but the income would come in that bracket. It indicates how seriously we affect people when we increase taxation in the lower income brackets. Generally speaking, incomes below $3,000 a year are those of the men and women of Canada who are carrying the burden, who are raising the men and women who will be the fighters or producers-or who are not raising them, and who very probably will not raise them, as the leader of the opposition pointed out. Under the circumstances I find it difficult to see why the minister bore down with such particular care on the people with lower incomes. He would answer, I believe, as I think he indicated in his speech, that since money had to be raised it was necessary to go down to the incomes of the people who constitute the majority of the population.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is an even and fair
gradation from $660 right up to $500,000.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But the evenness
ceases to exist when you get into the realities. It is easy to say that academically, but it certainly is not true when you get down
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

into the lives of men and women. The people with those incomes are having all the trouble to get along that they need.
The minister, still indicating that he was desirous of being equitable, said, as I recall it, that he desired to see people have a decent standard of living. Now, what is a decent standard of living? "Decent" is one of those general expressions, like "a fair wage," "a fair price." It means pretty nearly anything, depending upon who uses the expression and who hears it used. If we could only come to some sort of agreement as to what constitutes a fair income and a decent standard of living! As an example, we felt it necessary, if I recall aright-I am speaking entirely from memory -to give a cost of living bonus to civil servants getting less than $2,000 a year. That indicated the belief that a decent standard of living would be rendered possible for the civil servant only by an income of not less than $2,000 a year. I rather think that is about right. But how in the world are the people who are getting $400 to $450 to have a decent standard of living? Yet we are taxing those $450 incomes through the sales tax right along. I think in a recent issue of the Ottawa Citizen there was a statement covering a considerable number of civil servants recently appointed all across Canada. A substantial percentage of them are girls receiving very small incomes and having a hard time to live in Ottawa and elsewhere. But the average income of all of them was $168 a month if I remember correctly. A man could live reasonably well on $168 a month, but if that is the average, when you take into consideration the large number receiving only a bare subsistence, there must be some receiving very substantial incomes. Probably they have no difficulty in attaining a decent standard of living, but I am not so sure about a good many others throughout this land, in agriculture and among the labouring people. What is a decent standard of living? I will not take time to go into it now; I simply raise the question. But I think it can hardly be assumed with justice that this budget is equitable.
This budget makes one more long stride toward the destruction of democracy through national debt. It increases our debt $2,228,000,000, according to the statement of the minister, as compared with $414,000,000 estimated increase for the past fiscal year. Our debt on March 31, 1942, was $4,062,372,000. It is impossible to forecast what our debt will be within a few years. Mr. J. H. Fisher, staff writer for the Toronto Telegram in an article on June 29, 1942, estimates that we shall be in debt to the extent of twelve billion dollars if the war lasts for three years, and I think we can pretty

safely assume it will last that long. That is twelve billion dollars as compared with three and a half billion exclusive of the guaranteed Canadian National Railways debt at the outbreak of war. Mr. Fisher estimates that this will constitute a mortgage of a thousand dollars a head on every man, woman and child in Canada.
I ask this question: Where does any man in this house or outside it suppose we are going to get the money for social services after the war, with a debt like that?

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who owns the debt?

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We will come to that in a moment; the question only aggravates the position. Whence will come the reward for the fighting men who are now risking their lives and being maimed? Where will preparations for a later war come from?
At this point I wish to pause to say something I have wanted to say a dozen times. I am going to say it now. I do not believe since the beginning of time there ever was a generation so callously betrayed by its leaders as was the generation which to-day is fighting for its life. Why? Because they had so big a debt they had to save; and the life and very existence of 650 million people are now in jeopardy because we owed so many dollars we had to tighten our belts.
What is going to happen after this war, with a twelve billion dollar debt hanging round our necks, if we insist upon using the system of financing of which the minister now apparently seems to be irretrievably enamoured? Whence will come the relief from the depression about which so many economists running round the country take delight in terrifying the people? "We have to have a depression" they say; "surely we are going to have a depression". Even the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) fell into that foolishness. There is no reason why there should be a depression in this country. There was no reason for the last depression. It was deliberately and foolhardily manipulated by blind men.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And nearly destroyed us.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It did destroy us, unless we, by good fortune, come through t.he war successfully. And the very men who engineered that depression are the men who are responsible for the defeats this race has suffered and is suffering to-day.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They should be shot.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Shooting is too pleasant an experience for them. They betrayed us shamefully, culpably, reprehensibly, and they

The Budget-Mr. Blachmore
are all getting ready to do it all over again as soon as this war is over, simply because we shall be owing twelve billion dollars of debt.
Here is the astonishing fact: we in the House of Commons, responsible members of parliament, calmly and complacently contemplate such a situation as that. Only the odd person here and there rises to contest the claim of those who insist that we must carry on according to this financial system.
The minister made the remark that the size of the debt did not much concern us. So that we may have exactly what he said I shall read his words, as reported at page 3578 of Hansard:
It is not the size of the debt that is a matter of chief concern for after all it is an obligation of the people of Canada through their government to the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member had better finish it.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To be perfectly fair, I shall read everything the minister wishes to have read. He continues:
Rather, we are concerned about the distribution of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is that sufficient? I want to be perfectly fair. He says that we are concerned about the distribution of the debt. The distribution, I say, is going to be very largely the same kind of distribution we had after the last war. Men who buy war savings certificates and victory bonds, yielding to the urgency of high-pressure sales methods, and activated by an impulse of patriotism, will dispose of their holdings. Of course they will-to pay the corner grocer, or to pay the doctor for the last child, or perhaps to prevent foreclosure on a home.
Who owns this debt? I say solemnly and after consideration, that to say that Canada's public debt is an asset to Canada is to tell a pernicious half-truth, more mischievous than an obvious falsehood. I know who made that remark, and I mean every word of what I have said, and apply it to him. In the position he occupies he should have had a stronger sense of his public responsibility than to make a remark like that, one which would deceive the people of Canada.

speechtext: It is just like reading only part of what I said.

speechtext: Would the minister put on record what Mr. Towers did say in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

The hon. member is attacking the governor of the Bank of Canada in unrestrained language because he had pointed out an obvious fact, namely that a debt is an asset as well as a liability. It is an asset in the hands of the creditor and a liability to the debtor-both of whom are Canadians.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My next words will answer the minister completely. The minister implied the same thing in the remarks I have just read into Hansard.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
