subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But taxes in accordance with their ability to pay. The rich will no doubt be taxed much more heavily than the poor.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I challenge the minister's statement that they are taxed in accordance with their ability to pay. The tax structure erected in this budget is there to stay, just as the three-cent postage tax, imposed at the time of the last war, has stayed to this day. Whether or not the people go down into the depths of degrading poverty, as they did during the depression, they will still pay that tax, just as we had to pay the three-cent postage in the depths of the depression in 1932 and 1933. There is no way of getting out of it.
This tax structure is being prepared to bleed the Canadian people of every last drop of spending power possible of extraction from their emaciated bodies for the next generation. And what for? To pay 3 per cent interest on a twelve billion dollar debt to a few favoured ones.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On what?
3S04
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On a twelve billion dollar debt, on the assumption- that the war will continue for three years.
The difficulty lies right here. With the exception of, I believe, only three, there is not a newspaper or a public official or a bank manager anywhere in the dominion that is indicating even the slightest scintilla of vision as to what can be done so as to change the system to a point which would render such intolerable conditions more endurable. All they do is to sneer at anyone who has any idea as to what might be done. They will not even go so far as to consider a suggestion and permit intelligent and honest discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the debt should be $12,000,000,000, which I do not admit for one moment, the interest would be $360,000,000. Why does my hon. friend say that we shall have to maintain these taxes because of the interest charges, when this year we are budgeting for expenditures of ten times what the interest charges would be?

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a very fine answer and a perfectly honest one. If the depression which is promised so abundantly and with such sincerity and gusto occurs, the productive capacity and the national wealth of this country will fall off in huge swaths, as it did in 1929, 1930, 1931 and 1932. The only way by which we shall be able to raise enough money to service that debt will be by the imposition and maintenance of such a tax structure as this, a tax structure which the people are now viewing with apprehension.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I do not admit the inevitability of a serious depression, although my hon. friend may,	*

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should be glad to have the minister explain that. I realize that he would not be prepared to explain it now. Public debt like private debt limits freedom of choice-which means a limitation of democracy in the case of the state,-a limitation of freedom and a limitation of choice of action. Public debt will threaten and completely destroy our security and will almost inevitably impair our productive power. The
[Mr. Ilsley.l
federal government could and should adopt such a fiscal policy as will enable and encourage all individuals and all groups of individuals to get out of debt and to stay out of debt. The present fiscal policy of Canada motivates and to a considerable degree necessitates falling into debt.. Ours is a debt creating system, and terrible have been the results.
I should like to refer to what has happened in Saskatchewan, and I quote from the United Farmers of Canada information bulletin of March, 1942:
In the meantime the farm debt in this province has increased by nearly $50,000,000 since the war commenced, thereby increasing the Saskatchewan farm debt to approximately $630,000,000 or $21 debt average on the
30.000.	000 acres cultivated in this province, which requires about $44,000,000 to satisfy interest. It is estimated that the average debt on the higher quality wheat land is $30 per cultivated acre. It should be remembered that much of this land operates the practice of summer-fallowing one-half of their land each year, consequently each crop acre in such circumstances carries a debt responsibility of $60 per acre, requiring $4.20 to satisfy interest obligation. And, granting that this type of land yields more bushels than the average land of the province, it would require about 45 per cent of a wheat crop at present prices to satisfy interest upon the debt.
That is individual debt.
Land of inferior quality is not in any better position because, while two-thirds of the cultivated acres is usually cropped and as the average yield is only about 12 or 13 bushels per acre, even with a less than average per acre debt, it is estimated that almost the same percentage of the wheat income is required to cover the interest amount.
As mortgage companies call for one full third share of the crop to apply as mortgage payment it should be clear that even this full one-third is insufficient to meet the interest obligation. Inis deficiency, plus an amount less than the one-third which also cannot be paid except in exceptional years is pyramiding upon unpaid principal. 1940 produced the second higher provincial farm income since 1930. i.e., $142,000,000 and in that year $42,000,000 was required to service the farm debt of this province, leaving about $100,000,000 as the fundamental maintenance for our provincial economy, or slightly over $100 per person.
It may be contended that this hardly has a bearing on the budget, but I shall soon show that it has. In Alberta, in 1935 the provincial debt amounted to $161,000,000; municipal debt,
570.000.	000; mortgage debt, $200,000,000; private debt, $171,000,000, making a total of
5602.000.	000. Those men who with complete ease and real satisfaction talk about our servicing this $12,000,000,000 debt forget entirely the other debts in Canada which must be serviced as well. In consideration of the debt situation which this budget is imposing

The Budget-Mr. Blnckmore
upon the people of Canada, and for other reasons, I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell):
That all the words after "that" in the said motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house views with alarm the obviously decisive drift into national or state socialism everywhere in evidence in this budget as indicated by the shackling taxation structure it erects; the sweeping trend towards centralization. bureaucracy and oligarchic regimentation which it involves and the general deterioration of morale and incentive to productive effort which it aggravates;
Further, this house regrets the government's apparent inability to see the vast improvement in Canada's efficiency that could be effected by a wisely scientific use of her credit and currency potentialities, and deplores the government's persistent failure to employ Canada's credit and currency to supplement her pay-as-you-go policy, thereby to restrict the appalling growth of debt, and to provide a means of gradually paying off Canada's indebtedness.
Therefore this house respectfully urges the government to formulate and to introduce at the earliest possible moment such a modernized credit and currency policy as will, to the greatest degree rendered possible by our available facilities, curb inflation, control debt, mobilize Canada's resources for total war, ensure democracy and security to Canadians, in war and then in peace."
I wish to turn now to another aspect of this budget. Indirectly this budget is an inflationary budget. There are many situations in life where a man trying to avoid a certain thing runs directly into it. The effort here is to avoid inflation, but this budget is inflationary in effect. In the first place, it actually forces up prices. Take fountain pens, watches, clocks, passenger fares, long distance telephone cafls, telegrams and so on as an example. It is commonly assumed without reference to the facts of the situation that each and every one of these items is necessarily a luxury. Are we to assume that people, no matter how poor they are, are now to be able to avoid travelling on railways? Are they not likely to need to use the long distance telephone? For example, take the man operating a small grocery store. Will people no longer require to send telegrams in case of death or great mishaps? Are the teachers in our schools to go henceforth without watches? Must the little nurses in training, no matter how poor they are, get along without watches? Are the children in our schools to be made to go without fountain pens on the assumption that they are a luxury? The price added to the cost of these commodities will increase the family cost of living.
The result is there will be a tendency toward inflation. That is not the most serious aspect of the situation. This budget will discourage
production, or it will, in many instances, render production impossible. Just as soon as production begins to be restricted, as it undoubtedly has been now in many respects, there will be an increased buying pressure on the price ceilings. A scarcity of goods always results in an increased buying pressure on the price.
No producer can continue to produce at a loss. The minister said that we would have to find another incentive than the profit motive to encourage men to produce. There are simply tens of thousands of men in this country who must have a little profit or they can no longer produce. How is it that so many men overlook that important fact? As soon as the producers of this country find themselves unable any longer to make a living they will sell their stock, if they are stock raising, desert their farms and join the army or go into industry or go on the streets and hawk. They will do anything rather than stay on the farm where they are losing money, for they must do so.
But once cattle are gone it takes a long time to recover them. We have one fine example of that within the memory of this house. A few years ago the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) deemed it expedient to allow a large percentage of the cattle in Saskatchewan to be destroyed. Would it not help wonderfully if we had those cattle back now? But they just are not there, and we cannot get them there; they are gone. Every herd of cattle that is slaughtered as those were slaughtered that we heard about the other night from the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) means another herd of cattle gone; and it does not matter whether the children of Canada were crying for milk or the children of Great Britain were starving for cheese, when the cattle are gone, production from them would be impossible, no matter how high the price of milk or cheese may be. Why is it that men cannot see these things in this most trying time? I find myself afflicted almost with dismay when I read some of the shortsighted statements which have been made by certain permanent officials, whom I am not now going to name, with regard, for instance, to the desire of the Ontario farmers for an increase in milk prices to enable them to produce or of the Ontario berry producers for a similar increase in price to enable them to produce.
The government of this country should be watching every breeding animal. Three years ago I pointed out to this house that no more female lambs should be allowed to be killed until we were certain we had enough. Would
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

it not be a fine thing if we had those lambs to-day? It would help our wool situation greatly. But there were all-wise who thought I was just foolish in making that suggestion. They will now continue to bump their heads against the cold stones of reality until they realize that once in a while some good thing can come out of Nazareth.
The government should be watching every heifer, every cow in this country, and1 seeing that none are destroyed until we are positive that we have all we need. That does not mean passing a law fdrbidding their slaughter; it does mean that the government would make sure of buying them if it was necessary for their owners to sell them. That is just common sense. There will be great pressure to sell and to slaughter unless an incentive is given to keep this stock, far more incentive than is indicated in this budget.
May I spend just a moment on inflation. I have spoken on inflation so many times in this house that I know everybody is weary of the subject. Nevertheless the fundamental facts regarding inflation which I have laid down since 1936 are the essentials upon which must be based a new economy, and every year of development will show the truth of what I say.
I am told that in one city of Ontario where there is plenty of ice in the winter, a number of companies, because of impositions and levies and restrictions of one kind and another, have been forced to close their ice business, after having been engaged in it, some of them, for sixty years. And this is all because of utterly impossible regulations. They were forced out of business, not because they did not want any longer to produce ice, not because there was not plenty of ice, not because people were not needing ice, but just because the officials in charge lacked the understanding and discernment, and the humility to be told. They had to go on blundering and bumping their silly heads until knowledge was knocked into them. There are some people that one cannot tell anything to-they know everything-until, by their immeasurable folly, they drag the people of Canada into misery. The result of forcing those people out of the ice business is now a scarcity of ice in that city. A scarcity of ice means that there will be a buying pressure upon ice and a tendency for the price of ice to go up; and if people are unable to buy ice, they will have in their pockets the money they would have spent on ice and will buy something else with it, which will bring pressure to bear on other commodities and cause an inflationary tendency.

Once we understand what inflation is and realize that it is not a great big ugly bogeyman, with cloven hoofs, a long tail, and great horns; once men realize that it is just a common-sense thing, the result of scientific facts, they will stop talking much of the indescribable nonsense which is being talked over the radio and in the press to-day, and they will come to realize that if we want to prevent inflation we must do the common-sense thing we would do if we wanted to prevent a headache-just refrain from the cause. The cause of inflation is a lack of goods, and anything that causes a lack of goods will have a tendency toward inflation. The people who made the regulations which caused these firms to go out of the production of ice were unwittingly doing that thing which was tending toward inflation. The people who unwittingly neglected to provide adequate sugar supplies in Canada were doing that which tended to cause inflation. The men who neglected to save the ewe lambs so that we would have plenty of wool in Canada were doing that which tended to cause inflation, and the people who caused the destruction of beef cattle all over western Canada were causing inflation and a rise in price without knowing it.
We need to look upon every dollar that goes into circulation as an agent tending toward inflation. As soon as it is out of circulation, it ceases to have that tendency. It is like a billiard ball that goes bouncing about a billiard table knocking anything that gets in its path and giving impetus to it. If you want to stop that billiard ball from doing more damage you must pocket it, and so with that one dollar bill. Get it into the bank, and then you will stop its inflationary tendencies. Every time it buys goods it tends to go into the bank. Suppose it is used to buy milk. The farmer who sells the milk will take the dollar and pay his debt that he incurred when he borrowed the money to produce the milk, thereby killing the dollar for that cycle so far as its inflationary tendency is concerned. If you want to avoid inflation, get as many goods and in as wide a variety as possible; get great productive capacity, and then the dollars which are out in circulation will find the goods and buy them and thus lose their inflationary impetus. Once people all recognize this simple, fundamental, common-sense fact, they will stop talking much of the foolish nonsense and indulging in much of the unjustifiable fears that we hear of to-day regarding inflation, and men will have a great deal more sense about money than many people seem to show in Canada. The government must take all possible care to see that there is plenty of goods in wide variety.

The Budget-Mr. Blachmore

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for warning me.
If we are to be saved from inflation, in large measure we must look to our farming population in Canada. The minister has, in my opinion, been unfair to the agricultural portion of our population. He may consider that that is a severe thing for me to say, but I say it in all calmness, certain that I am right. He has been unfair to the agricultural population; he has slighted the farming population, perhaps without knowing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not in the budget.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, surely in the
budget there should have been some provision made for more generous treatment of the farmer, if the minister was aware the farmer was needing it.
It is a strange thing that the minister should neglect this important matter in his budget, because in speeches which he has delivered in the past he has made statements indicating that he was aware of the importance of agriculture in our economy and the bearing of agricultural production on the whole question of monetary policy, of our strength to win the war. May I read passages from a speech which he delivered before the Ontario Federation of Agriculture on March 17, 1942. I read particularly these words:
The important position of agriculture, indeed its central position, in relation to this whole policy of price stabilization, -was recognized from the very beginning.
Well, we certainly have no evidence that it was, from the prices that were given. I continue to quote:
As I emphasized in explaining the programme to the House of Commons, the policy could not be introduced until farm prices had been allowed to come fairly well up in line with other prices. We had waited until this had happened. By the time the price ceiling was put into effect the general level of retail food prices and of farm prices, with the exception of w-heat, had reached a fairly reasonable relationship with other prices.
Did the minister really believe that? If so, he was altogether misinformed by the men who advised him. I think the minister has some particularly doctrinaire and academic advisers. I think he should get some people from the fighting line of production, where they know something of the realities, to mix with these doctrinaire gentlemen who have taken university degrees and thus are supposed to be qualified to be the minister s advisers in these trying times. Again the minister says:
Let me assure you, however, that the arrangements by which the prices of various agricultural products are controlled have been worked out, and will continue to be worked out, by men who understand farm marketing problems.
These men may understand farm marketing, but they appear not to understand farm production.
On the prices board itself we have two senior representatives of the Department of Agriculture, and as foods administrator we have been fortunate to be able to secure Mr. Taggart, Minister of Agriculture of Saskatchewan, an outstanding authority on farming. Under lnm are many other experts on the marketing oi farm products to work out methods and details in consultation with producers and distributors.
I wonder how many on that board are practical farmers, who have got right out and known what it takes to produce a pig, what it costs to produce a bushel of wheat, who know the effort and expense it takes to produce a dozen eggs and keep on producing eggs.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Taggart himself
does.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Then he must be the only one. There is no evidence that these men-and I do not know one of them except Mr. Taggart, whom I met once-are aware of the real needs of agriculture in this country. There are too many factors which they are disregarding altogether. I shall refer to one or two of them before I finish. Again I read: For most of us who are civilians that means one thing above all else now; to produce; to produce more rapidly, to produce more efficiently.
True. The minister never used truer words. It is to our superior productive power that we look for an overwhelming victory. We must make that power effective in the factory, in the mine and forest, and in the field. We must produce the goods and deliver the goods.
Utterly true. The one means of producing the goods is to make it pay to produce them. You do not need to go out and plead with farmers over the radio to be patriotic. If you make it pay them to produce goods, they will produce them, if you make it pay them so that they can live.

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
Having quoted the minister's speech in March of this year, may I quote from his speech on the budget, as reported in Hansard at page 3592:
The war will not be won by disputing as to whether labour or agriculture or employer or employee should get a larger share of a swollen national income.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Perfectly true, but the war may be lost by disregarding the economic exigencies of the whole process of production. It. may be lost, I say, by ignoring these things. Men will plead only so long. All that the minister and the men who are associated with him need to do is to read the remarks which were made by the leaders of the delegations who have come in the last three weeks to this government pleading for consideration. Read those statements and see how much hope there is in them. See how nearly ready these men appear to advise that men should stop milking cows and go and join the army. If, Mr. Speaker, we are not going to dispute about matters such as these vital ones to which the minister has referred, why all the prattle about equity? If we are going to pay handsome salaries to civil servants to take lucrative and dignified positions from one coast of Canada to the other, while we tell the farmer that he is supposed to produce for solely patriotic motives, I think the gross inequity will appear so grotesque as to arouse the disgust of ordinary men.
All one has to do is refer to the beef situation. I come from one of, I believe, the best beef-producing constituencies in Canada. What an amount of significance there was in the question asked this afternoon by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox (Mr. Tustin) why the packers were permitted to lower the price of beef.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Never for a moment should that have been permitted. Who is governing this country? Is it the dominion government or the Canada Packers?

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

If Canada Packers are able to dictate prices and decide whether this country is to have production or is not to have it, how long can we maintain that we are governing this country intelligently? How long can we maintain that we are guided primarily by the principle of an all-out war effort? I speak as one with experience. My father and my family have been producers of 
beef since I was old enough to know what a cow was. The beef prices in this country have been such as to ruin the beef producers; and now, at the very time when they have a chance to recover themselves, to improve their breeding stock, to get pasturage, to repair their fences, we have Canada Packers obtruding its unwholesome self into the picture, and the government sitting supinely by and permitting it, and then talking about governing the country.
We have to have discussions of farm income, and the discussion should have been on the floor of this house. I have avoided carefully saying anything in this plebiscite discussion which might embarrass the government, or might indicate that I did not sufficiently understand the situation. I will grant that there are things no man can understand, coming from the wholesome west here to Ottawa where we have to hear about the most pernicious political sculduggery going on. I have deliberately avoided saying much about this plebiscite, but it has been one of the astonishing things of my life that this government has devoted months and months to a discussion of the plebiscite and has never had any time to discuss the price of beef which meant food for Britain.

That is
playing politics pure and simple.

Playing politics, as
the leader of the opposition says, and then having the effrontery and hypocrisy to maintain their concern about an all-out W'ar effort, That is the thing that amazes me. I would say that the minister showed callous disregard of the interests of the farmer. He may not have felt it. but it was there and there was the insinuation that farmers should not busy themselves about incomes, about their share of the national income. But you can appoint deputy ministers at $9,000 a year!

And take it away
from them in income tax. .

speechtext:
Yes, but you will be taking it away from the farmers in income tax if they get it. At any rate it would be a little comfort to them to be able to get it. The minister in his speech manifested little appreciation of the difficulties of the farmers. There seems to be a surplus of highly paid individuals going to and fro in Canada nowadays calling upon farmers to produce from patriotic motives. Why not help them to make their efforts yield returns? Here is an evidence of the attitude of such men who pose as financial and economic advisers to the people of Canada in this grave crisis. I quote

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
from the letter of the Bank of Nova Scotia of March, 1942, from which I gathered a great deal of understanding that helped me to see through some of the government ways. I quote:
The price of wheat is a matter of national policy. Such policy must take into account the fact that, from a war-time standpoint as well as from a social standpoint, all sections of the population should receive enough income to maintain their health, their efficiency as producers, and their morale. But such policy must also take account of the fact that war is a time of shortage and that financial assistance to any group increases the demand of that group upon the diminishing supplies of manpower and materials available for civilian purposes.
The income of a deputy minister apparently does not have any effect upon the demand for materials, nor do the incomes of those officials appointed to lucrative positions across Canada apparently affect the demand for materials. But the moment farmers get an extra dollar, that affects the demand for raw materials for civilian supplies. Is it hypocrisy, or is it just unbelievable inconsistency and lack of intelligence?
To continue:
These two considerations balanced against one another, rather than the more obvious financial aspects, set the real limits on aid to prairie wheat farmers-
This indicates that the prairie wheat farmer must be content with only 90 cents a bushel for wheat, not because the government cannot pay more, but because the government is afraid to let the farmer have the money to spend. He is likely to hurt himself and Canada if he takes the money and spends it or pays off some of the tremendous debts that exist in Saskatchewan, or those great debts in Alberta, or pays his store bill or his doctor's bill which has been standing for ten years as a result of the depression. If the farmer takes the money for any of these purposes, he will cause inflation. Can you beat that in this time of war, in 1942? I continue the quotation: -or for that matter, to any other depressed group of the population.
That is an acknowledgment that the farmers are a depressed group, and we have the callous affirmation of the proposal to keep them a depressed group purely because they must not have the money for the reason that it would cause inflation. That statement comes from the Bank of Nova Scotia in its March, 1942. letter. That man should be made chancellor of one of the prominent universities in order to be quite consistent with what has gone on in the past in Canada.

speechtext: He ought to be in the Bank of Canada.

speechtext:
Let us see what the farmers think about this matter. I will read what George W. Robertson, Secretary of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, has to say. He is a man who knows what the realities are:
In my judgment the establishment of parity prices for agricultural commodities represents the equitable method of price control for the agricultural industry, and that no price ceilings on farm commodities should be established below parity level. I would define parity prices for farm eomodities as the price which these commodities would need to realize in order to purchase as large a quantity of other commodities now available as it actually did during a specified base period, preferably 1926 to 1929. Ceiling prices should be established at levels approximately 15 per cent above parity prices to offset increased living costs recognized in government's labour policy by provision for cost of living bonus.
It will be answered that price parity has been established, but I will prove unchallenge-ably that it has not been established.

After Recess

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before the dinner
recess, Mr. Speaker, I was dealing with the budget and arguing that the farmers were not receiving a fair deal. I said' that the minister has slighted them, that he had disregarded their interests, that in his budget speech he had indicated a rather callous attitude toward them. Whether or not I was fair to the minister I am not able to say; we shall be better able to judge that by what he does in future, rather than by anything he may say now or anything he has done in the past. I was pointing out that the farmers generally were under a very heavy burden of debt, and now I wish to go forward with the argument as to whether or not the prices the farmers are now receiving are equitable. -
The minister indicated that the farmers were receiving reasonably good prices and a reasonably good income. But the minister, in saying that, disregarded the increased cost of the things the farmers buy. In order to show the truth of my statement I should like to read from the Searle letter of June 3, 1942. This letter is published by the Searle Grain company, which I believe is one of the best authorities on farming problems to be found in western Canada. I find the following remarks on page 1:
However, as was shown in an article in this letter on May 20, the price of wheat at the new 90 cent price will still be 31 per cent
The Budget-Mr. Blachmore

below "parity"; the price of hogs is now 15 per cent below "parity", of steers, 19 per cent above and of lambs, 11 per cent above "parity". ("Parity" meaning the present purchasing power of these products as compared with their same purchasing power over the same things farmers had to buy in 1913-14, all as shown by the Searle index.)
This indicates that on the whole the fanners are a good deal worse off to-day with respect to prices than they were in 1913-14. But may I pause here for a moment to deal with this whole question of parity prices. There seems to be abroad both in Canada and in the United States the idea that if we could' get the farmers back to the point where they would be getting the same income as they were getting in another given period of time, say between 1909 and 1914 or between 1926 and 1929, or some other period, all would be well with us and we would have no further need to worry about the farmers. I do not believe there has ever been a time in this country when the farming population has had a fair deal. There has always been the grossest disparity between the prices farmers were able to obtain for their products and the prices of things they had to buy. So to say that prices have returned to parity is not enough. We must place the farmers in a position in which they will be able to get as much for their effort, as much of the goods which other people produce and which the farmers have to buy, as other people are able bo obtain of the goods which the farmers produce and sell. Then, and not until then shall we have something like a balanced economy with respect to the farming population of this country.
May I now read another statement from the same Searle letter of June 3, 1942;
The Searle index of the cost of things farmers buy (147 items), now stands at 152-3 (1913-14 equalling 100). This means that these things cost farmers of the west at the present time 52-3 per cent more than did similar items of the same qualitv in 1913-14. (These costs have risen 16-3 per cent since August, 1939.) The price of wheat is now 10-5 per cent lower than it was in 1913-14. The purchasing power of a bushel of wheat is now, therefore, only 59 per cent of what it was in 1913-14.
When it is remembered that such a large percentage of the farmers of Canada, and particularly of the farmers of the west, are mainly occupied in the production of wheat and are scarcely in a position to go into any other kind of production, I believe such figures must give any thoughtful man cause for serious concern. But there are other matters which go still further in support of the statement I made. I have in my hand the booklet issued by the Searle Grain company, setting forth in great detail the costs of the 147 items which are used

by the company in compiling their index, indicating the manner in which the prices have increased by years from 1913-14 up to the present time. From this booklet let me cite a number of facts which I think should impress the members of this house. With regard to twenty-eight items of household equipment, taking the 1913-14 level as 100, it is true that whereas those items of household equipment were priced at 100 in 1913-14, prices had risen in 1926 to 165 and had risen still further in 1941 to 175. Of fifty-three items of farm equipment which were priced at 100 in 1913-14, in 1926 they were priced at 149, and in 1941 at 156. Of twelve items of farm machinery, taking the price at 100 in 1914, we find that price had risen by 1926 to 164, and bv 1941 to 187.
Nothing further should be necessary to indicate that even if it were shown that the prices the farmers are receiving had returned to the 1926 level, that in itself would not indicate that the farmers were receiving an adequate return having regard to the price of things which they have to buy as compared with the price of things they are producing and selling.
There were other matters which the minister disregarded, and which are likely to be disregarded by such good men as Donald Gordon and others, men of good-will but who simply have not had time, in the great urge of their responsibilities, to look into all the facts, and who have been advised by men who also are not familiar with the facts. The matters which might be disregarded include such things as these. Many of the farmers, as I indicated in my remarks before the dinner recess, have been forced out of live stock, so that now they do not possess the breeding stock which would enable them to go back into the production of beef or other commodities which might be more profitable to them. They have been through a depression and a long series of very bad years. As a result they have not the capital with which to go back into live-stock production, even should they wish to do so. Then in a great many cases they lack equipment, and in many more cases they are hopelessly in debt. They are simply hampered at every turn. Furthermore I believe the minister has overlooked the increased debt of the farmers, to which I referred at an earlier stage of my remarks.
Before I go on to the last aspect of the budget with which I choose to deal to-night, I wish to read to the house a line or two that will indicate something the minister might do in view of the precedent he has set in this budget.
The minister has forced loans from a number of people, and is undertaking to pay them

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
only 2 per cent on the money he is forcing them to place with the government. He makes the promise that he will return that money at the end of the war. There are gentlemen who lent money in the past throughout the west, and perhaps throughout the whole of Canada, at interest rates running up as high as per cent. It was largely as a result of those high interest rates that Alberta was reduced' to the state of financial impotence in which the Social Credit government found her in 1935. And it is largely because of that state of financial embarrassment that so many things have occurred under that administration which have aroused the indignation of so many people in high places in Canada.
I should like to read a passage from an editorial appearing in the Edmonton Bulletin of Monday, June 29, an editorial which I believe will need no explanation or amplification:
The high interest rates on public and private debt in Alberta is nothing short of a scandal. Alberta was faced in 1935 with bankruptcy, due largely to paying ruinous interest rates. The drastic action by the Alberta government in cutting in half, to two and a half per cent, the interest rate on the provincial debt was the only action possible at the time, unless social services were entirely abandoned, or by pyramiding a huge increase in debt by funding the unpayable interest charges.
Edmonton is paying about $500,000 yearly in excess interest charges. And still we hear the suggestion to raise street-car fares and curtail much needed civic improvements.
The place to direct our demand for action is where action is possible-the hon. Mr. Ilsley, Minister of Finance, has absolute power to remedy this deplorable situation, which is a positive menace to the public interest.
When Mr. Ilsley in his new budget compels Canadians to lend part of their weekly wages at 2 per cent interest, why can he not compel our financial corporations to charge only reasonable interest rates.
Edmonton is paying 150 per cent more on a debt of $26,000,000 than what Mr. Ilsley declares to be a fair rate of interest.
Canada is fighting for its very existence against Hitler's new order of world slavery, and cannot continue to support the "high interest racket" if she hopes to make an all-out war effort.
One might suppose that that was from a Social Credit paper; but it is just a good, hardheaded Liberal paper from Edmonton,

upon the term during which you have the money? Two per cent is a fair rate for a short term.

speechtext:
If this war lasts for
ten years the minister will not return the money until after ten years, and the 2 per cent will not be increased, I say to the
minister that 2 per cent is enough. And 2 per cent is also enough for these other gentlemen to have. If they need any more than the 2 per cent, then I suggest to the government that it direct the Bank of Canada to refund the money. Let it give those men back their money, and then let the people of Edmonton have the money at the 2 per cent rate. It does not make sense in 1942, for a people to be charged 5 per cent or 6 per cent on money, while other people are in the throes of war, and having to suffer in order to pay that interest.
I should like now to turn to another aspect of the matter discussed in the budget speech. I would point out that things should be ever so much better than they are indicated in the budget. Again I am not casting any reflection upon the minister. In view of the circumstances in which he found himself he probably did the best he could. So long as he holds to the ordinary debt finance system he is going to be forced to bring down more and more onerous budgets, year after year, until the people of Canada are completely crushed under the enormous structure. It is not so serious now perhaps when the government is spending huge sums of money for goods which are to be taken overseas and destroyed. But just as soon as the country has returned to an economy wherein it consumes what it produces, then there will be a collapse. The object of this group is to adjust our affairs before the time comes for that collapse.
I suggest that the budget could be a victory budget, instead of a budget of defeat, as it is to-day. Notwithstanding all that is going to be done with the money that is raised; notwithstanding the splendid effort Canada has made in the war-and I have no thought of disparaging its vast effort-Canada is not by any means doing what she is capable of doing, judged from the point of view of materials, men, and organization.
If business methods were applied directly to Canada's financial and public affairs we could have a great improvement. May I read to the minister something from his budget speech which possibly he hardly realized was so significant, but which I am going to point out to him as being very significant. This is what he said, as reported in Hansard at page 3578:
We can probably again draw on inventories of civilian goods but by how much I do not know, for information as to inventories is very deficient.
No expression could have been used on the floor of the house which would condemn the government more completely, beyond question, than that statement. The very first
*3812
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

thing a businesslike administration should do is to discover what inventories are from one end of the country to the other. When we had that make-believe registration, that child's-play window-dressing in 1940, there should have been a registration of every aspect of Canadian public life, a complete registration "of Canada's economic set-up. People will ask: How could it have been done? It could have been done. How is it that the bureau of statistics accomplishes so much by way of gathering statistics? Is it to be supposed that the bureau of statistics could not have been enlarged and specialized so that a complete inventory of everything in the country would have been prepared. Had that been done, the government would have been able to tell at a moment's notice- the minister himself, or anyone in charge of* his department-just how many shoes there are in stock from one end of Canada to the other, just how many pounds of butter there are, how many suits of clothes there are. Of course it could have been done. That would be a first essential in a businesslike administration in any country whatsoever, and especially in a country like Canada.
Without delay, the government should at once obtain an accurate and detailed inventory of all goods on hand, from coast to coast. Let it inquire into the amount of food, clothing, shelter, available fuel, educational facilities, available medical and dental services. Let the people be informed as to the available supply of those goods and services. The government would then be in a position to tell how much money it could put into circulation, without causing inflation. Then it would be able to tell how much in the way of goods is available for consumption, how many pairs of shoes a family may have, how many pairs of shoes the province of Alberta may have from Canada's supply, all matters which are vital to any government, where the money situation is going to be managed properly.
Then the government should know the number of non-Canadian goods, goods we receive from Great Britain, the United States, South America, Mexico and other countries.
We should know the number of goods in sight. For example, sugar is produced in my constituency. The government should know exactly the amount of sugar which it is estimated will reach the market this year. Probably it does know that-very likely, in fact, because there is a sugar controller. Then it should have the same information with regard to every commodity in Canada.

It should know the productive capacity of the country. The government probably does know the productive capacity with respect to sugar and a few other commodities, but it should know' the productive capacity with respect to every other commodity in. Canada. For that productive capacity has a direct bearing on the question of inflation, the question as to whether money must be taxed out of circulation, so that people may be kept from buying goods, and the question as to whether the minister should have forced loans, or should spend money.
The government, I say, should know the productive capacity of the country. It should know the mechanical productive capacity: the number of machines for manufacturing cloth, for example, and the number of machines for the manufacture of other commodities. It should have the extent of our transportation facilities. The government should know the extent of our storage facilities. This information should be right at the government's finger-tips. All that should be necessary in order to obtain the information is to touch a button. It could be done. The government should know, too, in great detail, the human material available in the country.
The government- should know the potential additional productive capacity. They should know, for instance, how much sugar could be produced, and how long it would take to get into that sugar production. They should know how' many factories it would be necessary to have, whether they could get the factories and all that sort of thing. They should know our honey producing capacity. They should know our wool producing capacity. They should know our dairy producing capacity, our fruit producing capacity and the same with all other foods. We should have full information as to the resources of Canada, both material and human.

There should be a complete inventory of the needs of Britain and the needs of Russia. Three or four times I have asked on the floor of this house to be given information as to how much of a given commodity the government wants. I do not believe the government has any definite conception of what it wants in the case of most of the major commodities which are required overseas by Britain and Russia. The government is so much in the habit of following the principle of laissez-faire that it cannot get out of the habit even to fight a war. It just has to let things drift. I think that situation should be remedied, and remedied at once. The government should determine what will be left for Canada after Russia, Britain and the other allies that require assistance have been supplied. Then after that it should determine what Canada's consumption could be.
There is something else that has been neglected by the government in connection with all these matters-the cooperation of the provinces. It is conducive to bureaucratic and centralized control in Ottawa when the wartime prices and trade board undertake to govern everything from Ottawa. They will find that in each of the provinces of the Dominion of Canada there is a government which is as much concerned about keeping prices down as ever the- government at Ottawa is. Those governments could be of great assistance to the wartime prices and trade board and to the ministers of the departments in making up inventories of goods and in doing many other things which must be done in this time of great peril. It would add greatly to our financial and economic stability.
Then the provinces could be divided into regions, and the regions could take care of these matters. The municipalities could take care of many things. I find that the cities are greatly concerned about prices within their own borders. They are just as vitally concerned as Donald Gordon or any other person in Ottawa in the prices of commodities. Surely we can count on the cities to assist most heartily and effectively in the administration of the policies of the wartime prices and trade board. I suggest that the government needs to decentralize its responsibility at once and bring in a great number of people to assist. It will have no trouble in doing that. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) is in his place to-night. He has mentioned that he has found the assistance given by the provincial governments and other bodies most excellent because they are all vitally interested in this war. They are not foreign countries; they are Canada, they are British. Why try to monopolize all the control and management in Ottawa? It just does not make sense. It is contrary to the spirit of the British North America Act. It is contrary to democratic procedure in any British country, and especially in a country like Canada.
After having obtained, with- the cooperation of the provinces, an absolutely accurate inventory of the goods on hand and the goods which could be put on hand at a given time, the next thing the government should do is to determine how much money could be absorbed by those goods and by services such as schools, dental establishments, medical establishments, tranportation facilities and all that sort of thing. The government should determine how much might be paid into debt and insurance before it fixes a tax structure such as the minister has fixed by this budget.
The government should next find out the prices which are necessary to stimulate the desired maximum production. I have said time and again that if you give a man a fairly remunerative price for his eggs, or any other commodity, I care not what it is, you do not have to go on the air and plead with him to produce that commodity. You do not have to plead with any particular producer to produce something that will prove profitable to him. As I say, the government should determine the price which will stimulate maximum production. If it is prepared to maintain that price, it will get the maximum production which it desires.
There is one more thing that ought 'to be done, something to which I referred1 this afternoon. Let us say the government is trying to determine the price that ought to be paid for

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

apples. There is no one in Canada who knows more about that price than the apple grower. Why not bring him into consultation instead of having a lot of doctrinaires who have probably never seen an apple orchard.
The next thing to do is to determine the wage rate which is necessary to stimulate maximum production and to make the labourer feel happy. When you are determining what your wage structure will be you should consult the workers; they know.

The minister can
hardly conceive how much reassurance he has given me by this evidence that he has finally got on to what is the right thing to do. That is the policy that should be followed. The people who are producing know what is necessary.
There is one more thing that should be done. An adjustment should be made in order to bring agricultural purchasing power, labour purchasing power and the purchasing power of each and every one of the other groups into harmony so that there may be balance in the economy of Canada. In his telegram to the Minister of Finance of October 14, 1941, Mr. H. H. Hannam suggested this and indicated quite strongly that there had to be balance in the Canadian [DOT] economy. Agriculture is only one of the groups. The other primary producers are . also groups; the wage-earners and merchants are also groups which must be brought into such a state of prosperity or spending power that there is a balance throughout the country.
The next thing, after having determined on the price, is to advance credit to producers who would produce and also to students who would be prepared to learn. I commend the government for having helped, through the Department of Labour, to train boys and girls for specialized work. This policy should be followed throughout the country. Wherever there is a young man who is qualified to become a highly skilled technician or workman he should be discovered and the government should advance credit so that he might be able

to go on and perfect himself, because that young man or workman can be made into a great asset.	.
Then there should be price subsidies and wage subsidies, and price discounts, pensions and other allowances. There should be subsidies for freight rates where necessary, and discounts of the prices of secondary products to enable farmers to buy.
People will ask: "Where are you going to get the money to do all this?" The members of the house know full well my stand on that question.
