speechtext:
Then I am going to say just a little bit more about it. The whole amendment which I have moved this day is centred around credit and currency management. In a country such as Canada it is possible to have a certain amount of credit and currency out in circulation; the amount of credit and currency that can be out in circulation depends upon the goods and services available, upon the consuming and producing power of the country. The task of the government is to determine by scientific means how much credit can be put into circulation without inflation, and then to see to it that that amount of credit and currency is put into circulation. The credit and currency should belong to the government, be under the direction and control of the government, and the direction and control should be exercised scientifically.
If the government wants a farmer away out in one of the Battlefords, for instance, to produce sheep, and the farmer has not the money to produce the sheep, the sensible thing for the government to do is to see that the farmer gets the money with which to produce the sheep, and to show him where he can buy the sheep. Then, when he produces the wool it becomes an asset to the country. If a similar principle were applied over the whole economy of Canada, the improvement in the national economy, in the wealth and strength of this country, would be almost inconceivable; I am sure of that. This whole matter of the possibilities of currency and credit management has been neglected by the minister up to the present; it is time he changed his ways in that respect.
I am going to give just one little illustration to show how this thing could be worked out practically. In Britain during the last war they created a credit instrument called the Bradbury and 354 million pounds of Bradburys went into circulation in Britain during the last war. Hon. members who are interested in a

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
study of the whole matter will find it excellently dealt with in "Currency, Credit and the Exchanges," by William A. Shaw, one of the best authorities on matters financial in the whole of Britain. As I said, 354 million pounds of Bradburys were distributed among the people. They were paper, treasury bills, nothing but paper currency, but they were accepted and they became legal tender. They helped to finance the war, and through them Britain won the war and would have won the peace had not evil counsels prevailed causing the discontinuance of the Bradburys some time after 1920.
We can think of saving certificates becoming legal tender just as easily as a five dollar bill. The savings certificates could be made not legal tender until a year from now, or two or three or four years from now. They could be kept out of circulation, "frozen" as it were, until the government saw fit to bring them into circulation by the simple device of declaring them to be legal tender or to be negotiable. The Bradbury experiment could be duplicated in Canada with great advantage. If we had a Canadian Bradbury and we paid the farmers the extra price necessary on his wheat with Canadian Bradburys or savings certificates; if we paid in Bradburys an extra price on any commodity that we chose; if we paid a subsidy on wages or on freight rates to bring down the cost of transportation of western wheat from the prairies to Ontario or Quebec or Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, the Bradbury or the savings certificate would then be being used as a credit instrument.
People will say immediately: "What good will all these things be to the companies concerned?" Well, what good are the savings certificates? What good is a bond, apart from the fact that it yields interest? A credit instrument such as the Bradbury or the savings certificate used in this way would be a use of the nation's social credit.
The number of Bradburys which could have been in circulation in Britain during the world war depended upon the number of goods and services available for purchase, together with the amount that could be produced. With price controls, the number of Bradburys could have been increased.
In Canada a considerable number of savings certificates could be put into circulation. What good would that do? Suppose the farmer received, at the end of the year, a 1500 subsidy in savings certificates, or in Canadian Bradburys if we decided to issue such a credit instrument. He could then use that credit instrument to pay off, say, a portion of a mortgage. The government could rule that 44561-241 i
the mortgage companies, but no other companies, could accept the Bradburys this year. That would enable the farmer to use that $500 immediately to pay off some of his debt. If a similar principle were applied throughout the whole economy of Canada, I think we would be astonished at the amount of debt that would be repaid and the tremendous amount of interest that would stop accruing, and surprised also at the general improvement in well-being and strength of the Canadian economy.
If the government chose to issue a kind of Canadian Bradbury or savings certificate it could say: "These certificates will not be transferable until the goverriment so proclaims by order in council". Then, if the government decided that it was unsafe to have that money put into circulation until three or four or five years after the war, it would be in a position to rule accordingly. The government would decide when they should be put into circulation. It need not be worried at all about inflation. If such an accumulation of purchasing power were put into the hands of the people as would result from the application of such a policy as I have indicated, we would have a fine guarantee against a post-war slump. When the war is over and we cease to spend money like water all over the country buying munitions, and the factories immediately tiy to transform themselves into peace-time production, purchasing power in many ways will at once cease to be distributed, and there will be a shortage of purchasing power, which will cause a shortage of buying, which will tend to cause unemployment and to bring on a depression. But if the government, knowing that there is a great deal of passive purchasing power in the hands of the people at this time, determined to use it by declaring that Bradburys or savings certificates, or whatever the credit instrument might be called, should be negotiable or legal tender at a given time, it would then have a reserve of purchasing power upon which it could draw to remedy the situation resulting from a falling-off of purchasing power following the making of the peace.
I wish to point out just one or two more things to hon. members. I am deadly in earnest in this matter; I am positive that there is a solution here, and that no solution can be found without some principle such as this. I crave the indulgence of the house to read into Hansard some bits of literature which I read into Hansard on May 25, because it is possible that some hon. members who are now here were not present when I read these passages before. I quote from a book called "Economic Tribulation", by Vincent C. Vickers, of the Vickers munitions corporation.
The Budget-Mr. Blachmore

To give an idea who Mr. Vincent C. Vickers is, I will read the following paragraph from the introductory note:
Vincent Cartwright Vickers was bom on 16th January, 1879, and educated at Eton and Magdalen College, Oxford. He was a deputy lieutenant of the City of London, a director of Vickers, Limited, for twenty-two years, and a director of the London Assurance from which he resigned in January, 1939. In 1910 he was made a governor of the Bank of England, and resigned this appointment in 1919. Eater, he became president of the Economic Reform Club and Institute.
I submit that any hon. member must be rather impressed by the record that this man has. It is 'not likely that a man of his calibre and his standing would recklessly espouse any untenable theory. In this book, which was finished on his dying bed, and published in 1941, and in which undoubtedly he put the very best things he had to say, he makes this reference to democracy, which I was discussing for a few minutes this afternoon. I then maintained that this budget is a step toward the destruction of democracy. As some hon. members might consider that I was extreme in saying that, may I support what I had to say on that occasion by the following quotation, which appears on page 66:
Our democratic system and our existing financial system can no longer live together; one of them must give way to the other.
And, Mr. Speaker, the one which is giving way in this country is democracy, and it is giving way very, very fast. I will read from the closing chapter of the book, in which the author offers suggestions which in his judgment are necessary for the preservation of democracy and the restoration of prosperity, peace and hope in the world, and particularly in his own beloved country. I read on page 74:
1.	State control and state issue of currency and credit through a central organization managed and controlled by the state.
In this dominion we could use the Bank of Canada. The minister told us not long ago in debate that he was using the Bank of Canada, but it was astonishing, I believe, to every hon. member-it certainly was to me -what meagre use he had made of its facilities. He had touched that privilege as though he was afraid of it. If he can use the Bank of Canada as a means of getting money without cost, as a debt to ourselves as a government, why not use it on a far more generous scale than that on which he has so far used it? If he feels that the financial stability of the Bank of Canada is not great enough to enable him to use it to help finance this war; if he feels that the responsibilities of that institution are so great, because of the foreign exchange control board and other

burdens upon it, I suggest that he establish in Canada a currency commission. Such a commission would not be seriously different from what existed in the last war. I pointed out to the house on a previous occasion that $26 million were printed in the last war by the treasury board for the cabinet and the Minister of Finance. That money was printed and used. Hon members will remember that up to the time of the organization of the Bank of Canada all the money of Canada was called Dominion of Canada bills, was printed and issued by the dominion treasury, and was,good money-as good as ever it has been since the Bank of Canada printed and issued it. To say that such a board cannot be set up in Canada to-day is to talk arrant nonsense. If the government feels that the Bank of Canada is not in a sufficiently stable position to issue this money, I suggest the appointment of a credit and currency commission whose business it will be to discover the capacity of Canada to absorb currency and credit without inflation and then issue that currency and credit and apply it scientifically in accordance with the needs of the people.
The next suggestion made by Mr. Vickers in his book is this:
2.	Stabilization of the wholesale price level of commodities.
He does not say how it is to be done. It can be done by a monetary technique, by price subsidies and discounts, as I have explained several times on the floor of this house.
That is to say, a fixed and constant internal purchasing power of money; so that a pound will buy to-morrow what it bought yesterday; an honest pound, not a fluctuating pound. And this can be done by so issuing and regulating the volume of available credit and currency that it shall at all times be adequate to permit of the purchasing power of the consumer being equated with the volume of production; not by limiting the purchasing power, but by firstly increasing purchasing power more in proportion to the productive capacity of industry.
Again:
3.	Fixation of foreign exchanges by foreign exchange equalization funds, and agreement with empire countries and all other countries willing to fall into line; and, once this was accomplished, the removal or diminution of trade barriers which to-day protect the countries from the results of a bad monetary system.
I pause there just a minute to point out, what I believe will be interesting to hon. members, that this writer says we have trade barriers because we have a faulty monetary system-which indicates that if we get a sound monetary system we can demolish trade barriers, greatly to the benefit of the people. I am not advocating any such set-up as will endanger our industries. We must have our

The Budget-Mr. Coldu'dl
industries in Canada; but we do not need to protect them by trade barriers; we can protect them with such subsidies as are necessary to enable them to compete successfully, and we can subsidize them by the creation of credit and currency which we are able to base on our goods-and-services-producing-power, which again is dependent upon our resources in materials and in men.
4.	Aliy additional supply of money should be issued as a clear asset to the state; so that money will be spent into existence, not lent into existence.
5.	The fluctuating quantity of gold lying in the vaults of the banking system should never be permitted to govern the volume of credit and currency needed by the country.
6.	The elimination of slumps and booms; and more direct procedure for eliminating unnecessary poverty.
7.	The abolition of the debt system where all credit is created by the banks and hired out at interest to the country.
May I in closing, Mr. Speaker, point out that there is no need for despair or for a defeatist attitude. This country is going to be richer after this war than ever it was before, except for the loss of precious men and women killed and maimed; for the riches of a country are to be computed in terms of the
goods-and-services-produeing-power of the
country. Every nation at present at war will be richer, excepting in those countries where productive power is being destroyed. The world is on the verge of a greater era of material prosperity than mankind has ever conceived of in its wildest dreams, and the only thing which can keep us from crossing the threshold and entering the realm of that prosperity is our own stupidity, our inability to adjust ourselves to the conditions of an age of plenty, our continuing to think we must carry on the affairs of this country in a power age with a dogcart or an oxcart financial and economic system.
What the government of this dominion needs above all things to-day; what the countries of the British empire and the united nations need above all things, is financially speaking, to turn and face the sunrise and cease to worship the sunset. Having done so; having modernized their economic and financial system, they may go forward with complete confidence; for our productive capacity far exceeds that of our enemies in combination. With the help of Providence, and our own good hard work, the work of the men and women whom we shall be able to employ as a result of a revised financial system, we shall struggle through, and under God we shall win, not only during the war but during the ensuing peace.
Mr. M. J. COLD WELL (Rosetown-Biggar);
I do not propose to speak at any great length to-night, because I believe that we should endeavour as far as possible to shorten this debate and to discuss in committee the various matters which we shall consider in connection with the minister's proposals. I am therefore going to confine my remarks within the shortest possible compass.
With what the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has said regarding the condition of agriculture both now and in past days I am in thorough accord. I do not propose to follow him and to discuss the other proposals that he has made; but, as I understand it, we are discussing a budget designed to restrict purchasing power among the people, and I think any policy which would defeat that objective would probably bring disastrous results upon the country at the present time. I, too, believe that we ought to plan our productive effort and our purchasing power in relation to one another; but to think that the mere issufe of more money will cure the ills of society, or that the mere manipulation of currency, credit and money will bring us into some sort of utopia, is to follow something of an illusion, a money illusion, if I may put it in that way; for, after all, goods and services, not monetary tokens, are the real wealth of a nation, and if mankind can once grasp that fact, I, like the hon. member for Lethbridge, believe that when this war ends we can be, if we will be, better off, happier than we have ever been in all our history.
I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) upon his able presentation of the financial position of the country. It was, I think, admirably done and he deserves every credit for doing such a splendid job. As a tax measure his proposals move in the right direction. I think they lag toward the top and fail to reach the objective that I should like to have seen reached. I think they fail, too, in another significant respect, and that is in the realm of social security. Again we have a war budget, a budget that contains no additional measures of social security, nor any additional help for the social security measures we now have in effect Old age pensions are left where they are; dependents' allowances are in the same position; veterans' pensions are too low with the rising costs of living which we have experienced, and I think that even in war time the budget should have recognized these needs. Indeed, I believe that if we are going to maintain the morale of our people, not only have we to consider the necessities of the aged, of the
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

dependents of men overseas and of a health programme for the nation, but we ought to provide something of a minimum standard of life for the people of the country. I should like to have seen a national minimum adopted and a ceiling placed on incomes, not as a political gesture but as a very real aid in our war effort, because I believe that while some sort of ceiling is being established now by means of heavy income tax in the higher brackets, the gulf between low incomes and those that remain high is far too wide.
The budget outlines stupendous expenditures-some $3,500,000,000 for the war alone; but in my opinion the Canadian people will not object to these expenditures because this war must be won, and in order to win it we have to produce the instruments of war. We have to arm the men who are going to the battle zones, and that means that we have to provide for the financing of the instruments of war and the men who>
will use them. The total budget, I say, is stupendous. With our peace-time expenditures it reaches almost the fabulous sum of $4,000,000,000. In spite of the very heavy increased taxation, just over 50 per cent raised by taxes, we have to Taise a very considerable portion by way of loans. Few will object to the higher income tax, because after all the income tax is probably the fairest way of assessing taxation in a modem country. Few will objbet to the increased income tax, provided they are convinced that these increases are made on an equitable and just basis.
In examining the minister's proposals in that regard, I was struck with the fact that the people in the low and middle brackets will feel the pinch most; for let us keep this in mind: it is not what you pay out in taxes that really counts; it is the amount you have left after your taxes have been paid that counts. On a $2,000 income the increase in tax and compulsory saving is over 250 per cent. That is a tremendous increase for a family man, we will say, in the $2,000 bracket to take all at once. In the $3,000 bracket the increase is slightly over 300 per cent. In the $5,000 bracket it drops; the increase is 120 per cent; and in the $10,000 bracket the increase is 65 per cent, while in the $50,000 bracket it is 30 per cent. The increase above $3,000 diminishes on a percentage basis as the income increases. I think I know the reason why the increase is so great in the middle brackets, but the impact of the present budget in the income tax field will be greatest in these moderate income groups. Presumably, of course, this is to restrict purchases of nonessential goods by the largest group of wage-earners and salary earners who can be reached

through the income tax. I know the minister can make a good case for the taxes, because he will say that the reduction in purchasing power in these fields is to prevent buyer competition, to prevent price inflation, and ultimately to release material and labour for war purposes. Those are good objectives, but let us not forget that the impact upon this group of middle-income earners is going to be very great indeed.
The introduction of compulsory saving is also a step in the right direction, following as it does to some extent the British plan, though I believe it is rather more severe than anything the British have adopted as yet.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You pay back more.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Quite right. A few moments ago the hon. member for Lethbridge remarked that the interest on these compulsory savings, which of course are in the nature of compulsory loans, is to be 2 per cent until paid, and it is anticipated that the loans will be repaid at the end of the war. Here, I think, is the defect in the minister's budget. Where is a compulsory loan made in connection with large accumulations of wealth, held either by individuals or by corporations? The owners of these accumulations will be induced to lend their money to the government at a rate, if the term is longer, in excess of the 2 per cent which will be paid those who are handing over their compulsory savings to the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But we take 20 per cent of the excess profits at no rate of interest.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will deal with that in a moment. I would point out that you are not touching the same people with your excess profits tax as I am talking about at the present time. I am talking about corporations, trust companies, insurance companies and individuals who may have large accumulations of wealth. They are not touched by the excess profits tax; we have no compulsory loan on those accumulations of wealth, and I think that is a defect in the budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will permit me, on their incomes we are much more severe than on the smaller incomes, in that we pay them back so much less.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Quite so, but I am not talking about individual incomes. I am talking about persons who have large accumulations of wealth, not income; and I am talking about corporations which may have accumulations on hand. I believe justice demands that where there are such accumulations, we should levy on them compulsory loans on a

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
graduated scale, according to their ability to contribute. The compulsory savings plan is, in my opinion, a good feature; but, like the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) this afternoon, I would say that I think it is bound to interfere with the sale of victory bonds in the future, and with the sale of war savings certificates and stamps. It will be impossible for the average man to pay the very high income tax, plus the compulsory saving, and also buy victory bonds and war savings stamps or certificates. Therefore I think the government and the country are going to face a very difficult situation in financing the amount which the minister indicated during his budget speech would have to be financed by way of loan, though I certainly wish him the very best of good fortune in endeavouring to raise money in that way. The amounts in the savings accounts of small depositors will be reduced, of course, and, as I say, that will make it difficult for such people to put their savings, as they have been doing for the past year or so, into various forms of war loans.
The minister mentioned the excess profits tax. It is raised to 100 per cent superficially, but in reality it is increased only 5 per cent, because 20 per cent will be refunded after the war. I think this is insufficient, particularly since the minister admitted in his budget speech that companies have been retaining substantial amounts for reinvestment in working capital, expansion and so on. I think, if I may say so, that this admission on the part of the minister in his budget speech is a vindication of all we have said in past months with regard to the necessity of a 100 per cent excess profits tax; and an answer, if I may say so, to the hon. member for St. Antoine-West-mount (Mr. Abbott), who a couple of weeks ago took me to task for picking out, as he said, a group of profitable companies. I may say I did not pick out a group of profitable companies; I took them more or less as they appeared in the newspapers, and somewhat at random, because they were war production companies. I say the determination of the government to impose this tax now indicates that the demand was justified when we made it some time ago.
With regard to the 20 per cent to be refunded, I noticed that this afternoon the leader of the opposition spoke at some length on this feature of the excess profits tax. He said that it would be a good thing; that it would enable industry to return to its normal way of doing things; that it would provide employment after the war, and so on. But I should like to point out to the house that the 20 per cent is to be refunded unconditionally.
There is no obligation upon the company which receives the 20 per cent refund in connection with the excess profits tax to do anything in particular with that money. It could, if it liked, cut a very substantial dividend melon after the war is over. This refund could, therefore, simply be deferred profits returnable to the shareholders when the war is over. If we are going to justify the return of this 20 per cent to industry when the war is over, that return should not be unconditional. It should be conditioned on industry using that amount in the transition from war-time to peace-time operations. Then this 20 per cent refund might be justified. Unless that is done, however, I would point out that we are simply setting up a fund out of which, at some future date, some nice, juicy dividends may be paid, and this would defeat the very object of the 100 per cent excess profits tax.
The leader of the opposition spoke of our little group and said he thought the worker was most interested in returning to his job when the war ended. He spoke at some length of the necessity of producing jobs for our men. Yet, as he was speaking-and I do not say this unkindly

I remembered that to-day is an anniversary. On June 30, 1935, in my home city of Regina, there were some 1,700 or 1,800 young men who were endeavouring to come to Ottawa to place their sad case before a government of which the leader of the opposition was then a member. I recollect meeting those boys in Regina and moving among them. In the number were university graduates and high school students. There were boys very much like my own boy at the time. What happened to them on that 30th day of June? In a peaceful meeting on the market square they were showered with tear gas bombs. A riot occurred, and one of our city detectives was killed.
Let us not allow that kind of thing to happen when this war is over. I have looked around the city in the past forty-eight hours and have seen the flags flying. The city is decorated in honour of those men who are now overseas-and I am glad the country is honouring those boys. Yet let me say that the greatest honour we can do them is to consider immediately how we may best give them an opportunity of living decent, comfortable lives when the war is over. To my mind, the flags are out of place until we have done something of that kind.
I said a few moments ago that the war will need every dollar we can find, and in my opinion we should go further in connection with the excess profits tax. We should take 100 per cent of all profits above a stipulated amount. In another debate in the house
The Budget-Mr. Cold well

recently I suggested that perhaps that amount might be limited to four per cent, and that above that we should take all else for the war effort. Indeed, I believe that would be fairer than the present system, because I think there is not a member in the house who does not know that in some respects the base upon which the excess profits tax is computed is both uneven and inequitable.
So I would point out that while we commend many features in the budget, it falls far short of anything which might be called the conscription of wealth in war time. It does nothing to conscript industry, and leaves financial institutions free to lend or to refuse to lend money to the government. In those respects, in my opinion it falls short of what a budget during war time ought to be. Let me emphasize again that it does not in any sense nationalize the financial system, without which, in my judgment, not even the shadow of the thing suggested by the hon. member for Lethbridge could be in any way instituted. Without a complete national control of the financial system it is impossible, to use the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to issue currency and credit in terms of the nation's need.
The Minister of Finance has also decided that the new income tax and the excess profits tax shall be collected at their source. I think that is a good plan, and will prevent evasion. But how does the minister propose to prevent evasion in respect of unearned incomes, incomes from all kinds of bonds and investments, unless he compels a complete registration of both the securities and the owners of those securities?
One of the good features of the budget is the allowance for medical care, nursing and that kind of thing. In view of the tremendous tax now imposed upon the Canadian people it seems to me that that is an essential accompaniment of the budget. May I say to the minister that I hope, when the regulations are drawn, they will be sufficiently broad to meet various types of cases. It is proposed to make provision for medical care, hospitalization and nursing services. Among many of the lower income groups there may be a sick mother in the home, or a sick member of the family, but those people are unable to engage the services of a trained nurse or to remove the sick member of the family to a hospital. Yet the amount they spend on the sick person may be very considerable indeed1. So, while they may not have the services of a trained nurse and while there may not be hospital expenses, there may be other expenses in connection with that sick person which ought to receive some

specific consideration by the minister. Regulations governing this matter are being drawn, and I draw this to his attention in the hope that he will give it favourable consideration.
Then, as in former years I want to put in a word of criticism with respect to the kindness which has been shown for a number of years to the mining interests in this country. I think they have been treated very generously in their relief from taxation. Yet we send out surveyors. I do not know how much the Department of Mines and Resources is spending this year in sending out geologists and scientists into all parts of Canada, looking for favourable indications of minerals or oil. There is no doubt, however, that a very considerable sum is being spent for these purposes. When we have located favourable areas the private companies come in, on most occasions do some further prospecting, and then exploit the properties for their own private gain. Then we give the claims to private corporations and individuals for their own profit.
I think the time has come when we ought to consider doing this ourselves, and obtaining from our vast mineral and other deposits all the revenue that is in them. I notice we are still going in for some prospecting in gold. Well, I agree with those people who think it something of a paradox that we should take gold out of one hole in northern Ontario, ship it to the United States and put it into another hole. It seems to me a great waste of human labour when we are at war, and labour is needed.
The increase in the tax on alcoholic liquors is, as the leader of the opposition said this afternoon, fully justified. I could only wish that some steps might be taken to bring about a more moderate use of intoxicating liquor at this time of war. I believe in temperance, rather than in total abstinence; but I look round this country, and it alarms me to see the amount of alcoholic liquors being consumed at the present time.
Taxes on such luxuries as cigars, cigarettes, tobacco and so on were to be expected, but I want to join with the leader of the opposition in criticizing the imposition of a fairly substantial tax on candies. I think some differentiation might be made. Where candies are worth more than a certain amount per pound or where they are put up in boxes, they might come under the tax, but I think exemption should be given to the ordinary fudges and hard candies which children love. I agree with the leader of the opposition when he says that children crave some sweetmeat. This is a natural craving, and candy in moderate quantities should be within their reach.

The Budget-Mr. Ferland
The people of this country must be given assurances of a greater measure of social security when this war ends. When peace is proclaimed, are we going back again to the old pre-war unemployment, insecurity and poverty? A mother of a western Canadian boy who is now overseas sent me an extract from a letter which he had written to her during the plebiscite campaign, and which I received about the end of May. The people are English born, and the boy enlisted early in the war and is now in Great Britain. He said he was surprised that I had advocated a '"yes" vote in the plebiscite. He stated that he and some other boys from the same city, all of English stock, had voted "no" in the plebiscite overseas. He said they voted "no" because they did not feel justified in compelling boys to go over there and, when the war is over, to return to the conditions that they left when they enlisted. That comes from a boy who enlisted voluntarily and is now serving overseas. That was his thought, and I am sure the same thought is in the minds of many thousands of Canadian boys who are now in uniform.
What are we doing in the way of real preparation for the post-war situation, for the boys who will come back from overseas and for the workers who will be dismissed from industry? We have unemployment now. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) will tell us that in the area which he represents miners are working only one day a week, and to-day they are enduring depressed conditions almost as bad, if not

speechtext: Worse.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member says worse than they had to endure during the years of the great depression.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend knows there is an answer for that.
