speechtext:
I know the answer, but I would point out that nothing is being done to assist these men to maintain their families in decency when they are on such part-time employment. What we need is at least some beginning of a comprehensive social and economic plan. Hon. members have said to me that they have not heard me speak lately of economic planning, but I want to say that it is always in my mind. I believe that there can be no intelligent social and economic, life in the future unless through our democratic institutions we build and plan effectively to meet the needs of the people. It is no good ciying "socialism! " That is like crying "wolf! " It can be cried too often. I remember not so many years ago when some people in Regina where I lived said, "This man, if given his way, 44561-242
will hoist the red flag on the city hall or on the grounds of the legislative buildings." Our former leader, Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, was accused in this house of wanting to put the red flag on parliament hill. Last Friday when I came up here in the evening I looked over toward the governor general's office and, hanging right outside his excellency's window, I saw the red flag with the hammer and sickle in the corner. I did not put it there. I want that to be known. Times are changing, and it is useless to cry "socialism".
I do not believe in stateism, whether it is state socialism, state capitalism or any form of stateism. In New Zealand the Labour government succeeded in having the foundations of democratic socialism incorporated into the constitution before war broke out. They hope to do this also in Australia under the leadership of Mr. Curtin, and they plan to do it in Great Britain when the war is over under such men as Bevin, Citrine, Morrison, Cripps and so on. Our social democracy must mean the preservation of the widest measure of private ownership in home, in farm and in those things which do not oppress the people, but taking into the nation's hands the great trusts and the great monopolies so that we may plan and use them to attain security, plenty and peace.
Mr. CHARLES E. FERLAND (Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to join the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell)- and the leader of the New Democracy group (Mr. Blackmore) in congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) on his brilliant delivery of a budget address remarkable both as to form and substance.
That part of the budget which introduces compulsory savings offers an interesting parallel with the "Enforced Benevolences" of King Henry VII who ruled England from 1485 to 1509 and who, impoverished at the end of the War of the Two Roses, filled the empty coffers in his treasury through compulsory loans levied from the nobility. But Henry VII never saw fit to repay his subjects the moneys he had forcibly extracted from their purse. Whatever the criticisms directed at this budget, Mr. Speaker, let us at least confess that our Minister of Finance is kinder than King Henry VII.
The two most important measures submitted to parliament during the present session are undoubtedly Bill No. 80, purporting to strike out section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act, thus introducing the principle of conscription of

The Budget-Mr. Ferland

men for overseas service, and the present budget in which the principle of conscription of wealth is incorporated' to a large extent. Canada's war expenditures last year amounted in round figures to a billion and a half. Now the Minister of Finance requires for the present fiscal period appropriations totalling yearly four billion dollars. He estimates the total revenues for 1942-43, the current fiscal year, at $2,050,000,000 and the total expenditures at the figure of $3,900,000,000. This would leave a deficit of $1,850,000,000.
The minister is relying chiefly on direct taxation of incomes and profits and on indirect taxation of goods and services to increase the revenues of the dominion by about $377,850,000.
Here is a summary of the budget:
First, a sharp increase in the income and national defence taxes is contemplated. These taxes will be combined and, whenever possible, deducted at the source. They will be increased by a salary deduction, considered as a form of compulsory savings, repayable after the war at 2 per cent interest.
Secondly, the excess profits tax is raised from 75 per cent to 100 per cent; 20 per cent of the tax would be refunded after the war also bearing interest at the rate of 2 per cent.
Thirdly, there are increased taxes on spirits, tobacco of every description, soft drinks, transportation, telephone communications, night clubs, luxuries such as furs, jewelry, candy, chewing gum, and so forth.
The Minister of Finance wishes the people to understand that Canada, together with the united nations, is in a critical situation and that victory will only be achieved after a long war. He said:
The war will be won, not alone by the valour of fighting forces and the skill of generals but by the willingness of the people at home to make necessary sacrifices-willingness to make those sacrifices first and not after all other groups have made them.
In this budget, the Minister of Finance calls upon the nation as a whole to accept the heaviest sacrifices in these tragic days, in this the most critical period of our history.
The budget has two main features: taxation is increased to such a degree that it appears crushing and savings become compulsory.
How will this war budget affect the 'economic life of Canada? I believe it is impossible at the present time, even for the exponents of new doctrines, the builders of theories, the pedlars of new systems and the experts who

contributed to the preparation of this budget, to foresee the consequences which, I fear, will spell disaster for many people.
Does this budget not preface a fundamental economic revolution? Is it not, to a certain extent, tainted by state socialism? Let us hope that it will not cause our economic structure to collapse.
This budget places our country on the same footing as every large nation devoted to an all-out war effort. I unhesitatingly state that Canada is now reaching the limit of her war effort, in spite of the statements made by inveterate conscriptionists who, during the last few months and even before, have waged a campaign of hate, prejudice, insult and slander against Quebec, ceaselessly proffering both in their newspapers and in public speeches, the same nonsensical charges with unheard-of violence and in a spirit of revolt against our province heretofore unknown in Canadian history.
Mr. Speaker, a nation with a population of 12,000,000 which raises an army of 500,000 men through the voluntary system, which can employ in its munition plants almost a million workers-the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) said that the figure was 900,000 at this time-which is able to maintain on farms at least one million men, which supplies to the common cause all the planes, the merchant vessels and the warships it can build in its yards operating to full capacity, which supplies all the guns, munitions, supplies and commodities needed by the allies, a nation of 12,000,000 which does all that has no reason to be ashamed of its conduct, and I do not hesitate to say that Canada now ranks with the great nations which are putting forth a total war effort commensurate with their resources. We are doing even more than our neighbours.
I have before me, Mr. Speaker, a table published in a Montreal newspaper showing the taxes proposed in this budget as, well as those that are paid in England and in the United States. I find, in the first place, that England pays the heaviest taxes and I wish to correct a wrong impression which I have frequently noticed among the working classes who think that Canada is doing more than England herself. Taxes are much heavier in England than they are in Canada. One can understand that because Britain is in the war zone.
There are a few comparisons: We find that while a single person with a $2,000 income is taxed $441 in Canada, that same person is taxed $624.50 in Britain and only $106 in the

The Budget-Mr. Ferland
United States. Single persons earning $10,000 in Canada must pay a tax of $4,312-not including compulsory savings-while in Britain the tax is $4,624.50 and only $2,190 in the United States. I will give no further illustration but the proportion is the same all along the line.
At first sight it does seem that this budget is bound to have among others the following results: it will so reduce the purchasing power of the people that the taxpayer, the consumer and the government's competitors will be unable to buy the raw materials required for war.
The general taxes and the 100 per cent excess profits tax will necessarily bring about a formidable, indeed an excessive reduction of wealth among the very rich. The middle classes will also be seriously affected and they will be forced to adopt a standard of living far below that of pre-war days.
I believe the farmers will not be affected by this budget, those of my province anyway. Such is also the opinion of a financial publication from Toronto. It complained in its issue of Saturday last of what it termed "a grave and serious omission." Still one would need to have very little knowledge of the conditions which obtain among the poverty stricken farmers in Quebec to state that they should be in a position to pay income tax.
Further examples make it evident that certain civil servants, bank employees, employees in industrial, commercial and other establishments, earning a $2,000 income, will find it very difficult to balance their budget particularly after having paid $450 in taxes. But the wealthy-and I emphasize this point as an answer to all demagogues who hold a grudge against the wealthy class-the rich man whose income formerly was $100,000 will only retain $21,000, that is 21 per cent, and turn over $79,000 to the state. And what about the millionaire with a $500,000 income? According to the budget provisions, Mr. Speaker, he will only be able to keep $37,000. On the whole, however, the class most affected is composed of people with an income between $1,500 and $3,000 a year. It seems probable that a large number of these people whose standard of living required every dollar of their income and who must continue paying the same rent until next May, will be unable to balance their budget.
I hope that the hon. Minister of Finance will, within the shortest possible delay, find the means to correct any errors that may have been overlooked in a war budget of that size.
I sincerely think that the present budget will inevitably lead us to the enacting of moratoriums which will necessarily be
44561-242i
requested of the government, especially by small property owners and a certain number of small industrialists doing business on a small scale, who seem to be seriously affected by the budget.
In order to reach its ambitious goal, the government also relies on a voluntary savings tax. Certain newspapers claimed1 that this was merely penalizing the thrifty, since the government taxes insurance premiums. Such a tax, although paid by the insurance companies, will necessarily affect the policyholders, for the companies will certainly deduct the amount of the tax from the dividends payable, at least in the life insurance field. Thus the people generally will be asked to make a further sacrifice.
I hold no brief for the wealthy, but I have heard so much said against them, especially by certain demagogues, that I would be remiss in my duty were I not,to point out to the house the sacrifices demanded of those who enjoy large wealth. Is it not true that the wealthy invest their money in insurance companies and are sorely hit by this new tax?
Many people who were in dire need before the war are now earning reasonable wages. A gradual levelling of the social classes is in process of accomplishment and1 it is to be hoped that after the war there will no longer be families in need of assistance, no unemployment in a country such as ours, as large as a continent and enjoying tremendous resources.
For this levelling of the social classes, the Liberal party deserves some credit. If we consider the results of the Unemployment Insurance Act through which the government collects from 50 to 60 million dollars annually, we must realize that these moneys are held by the state for the benefit of the working class and not for the rich.	[DOT]
Mr. Speaker, as I said before, the government is requesting our people to make tremendous sacrifices. In the opinion of the administration, the present budget is necessary to attain an all-out war effort. Although I find the budget provisions severe, I find war even less to my liking and our people would be even more harshly treated in the event of an invasion of our shores, in the east by Germany or in the west by the Japanese.
The Canadian people realize that in view of the immediate threat to our country and to all the united nations, every individual must do his part and accept personal sacrifices, and no one in our dominion can remain indifferent to the war effort directed by our government.
The Budget-Mr. Ferland

Mr. Speaker, as the representative of the three combined counties of Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm, with a population of 65,000 who have raised no objection to the government's war programme, who have accepted every measure with the sole exception of conscription for service overseas, I believe, Mr. Speaker, that I am expressing the opinion of virtually all my electors when I say that I shall support this budget on the whole, in spite of certain mistakes it reveals, mistakes which, I repeat, are unavoidable in a war budget of that size. I feel that the province of Quebec will accept this budget. I hope it will accept it without complaining. That is my personal opinion, for I have consulted none of my fellow members from the province of Quebec. We have taken that stand, but I feel that I am serving the best interests of my country and. my province in supporting this huge war budget, the largest in our political history. I feel that I would ill serve the interests of the French Canadians by a futile and barren opposition to this war budget which commands the general approval, as far as I can see, of the members of this house and which also seems to enjoy the approval of the press in this country. Of course I have no desire to force my opinion on hon. members. Every member of the Liberal party enjoys complete freedom. Those who do not agree with me are at liberty to take whatever stand they deem appropriate. I do not blame them in the least but I sincerely believe that ~we from Quebec would be mistaken in opposing such a measure; we would even interfere with the spirited battle undertaken by the members from Quebec under the efficient leadership of the former Minister of Transport and Public Works (Mr. Cardin) who has tendered his resignation, and who did1 a creditable thing when he showed the country at large that the province of Quebec is unalterably opposed to conscription. I feel it would be a mistake to persist in our quarrels and our dissensions on matters of lesser importance and that conscription must take precedence over financial questions. After all, as the saying goes, what money mars money will mend. And I assert with all my heart and with the utmost sincerity that there will never be any equality of sacrifice as between the soldier who sheds his blood, who gives his life, and the Canadian citizen who gives his money. I feel in duty bound to support the government on this measure. I am in agreement with the government's entire policy since the beginning of the war, and I will continue to support it with the sole exception of conscription for overseas service. I shall take the opportunity of stating why my electors are 
opposed to conscription at some other time, but for the time being I merely want to say that I shall vote against Bill No. 80.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay the business of the house much longer. This is army week, dedicated to the Canadian soldier. The government has directed that during the week extending from the 29th of June to the 4th of July, we should honour our valiant Canadian soldiers and, personally, I see no better way of paying tribute to the courage of our soldiers than by telling my fellow-citizens in the province of Quebec that they have a duty to fulfil and that if they are opposed to conscription, they must at least make personal sacrifices and assume the obligations imposed by this budget which is deemed necessary in the opinion of the government.
As an homage to the soldiers of Quebec as well as to the clergy and the bishops of our province who have supported every activity of the government with clear-sighted and broad-minded patriotism, may I be permitted to quote an excerpt from the collective letter made public by our bishop:
Let it be recognized that this spirit of devotion and self-sacrifice is nobly expressed by those who so courageously enlist in the army, navy and air force. We owe a debt of gratitude to our fellow-citizens who, by their courage and their bravery, will have so magnificently served their country and humanity. Their triumph over personal interest is a pledge of final victory: their loyalty honours our nation; their faithfulness to duty is the bulwark of our freedom. Every day we have new reasons to be prouder still of their steadfastness and their courage under fire, through thick and thin. They show themselves worthy of our young and valorous country. In their willingness to conquer or perish, their hearts are filled with heroic strength. And the sacred ties that bind them to all they hold dear are as many reasons for fulfilling their worthy part as defenders of our freedom.
So speak the bishops of the province of Quebec of the self-imposed sacrifices of our soldiers who are risking their lives and who stand ready to shed their blood for the common cause. Do our sacrifices count for so very much, I ask you. Would we not be ashamed to refuse to give a few dollars in support of so sacred and so dear a cause in this struggle between civilization and barbarism, in this battle of freedom against slavery?
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote these words addressed to our soldiers on the occasion of this national celebration, which I have taken from the newspaper Le Droit:
The Canadians are there!
. . . and when the Canadians are there, that means the enemy shall not pass! . . . What heroic deeds are theirs! . . . What perilous

The Budget-Mr. Church
tasks they have accomplished! . . . More than once have they covered themselves with glory by standing fast when it seemed impossible and in taking positions held impregnable! . . .
Stout hearts and valiant arms, the Canadians have their legend. Those of to-day are the worthy sons of those of yesterday, and blood will tell.
They shall hold fast and they shall conquer!

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Tomorrow is Dominion day, the seventy-fifth anniversary of confederation. I thought we would have been home long ago; and I think the time has come, after we have been here since November last, when the house as quickly as possible should conclude its business. I am only filling in, as it were, to-night as one member of the opposition in order that the debate may go on to-morrow.
In Sir John A. Macdonald we have one of the main pillars of confederation; he was one of the great statesmen who were responsible for bringing about that great event. He was Attorney-General of Canada, and we did not hear in those days the strange talk that we heard in this house the other day from one other Attorney-General of Canada, because, after all is said and done, Sir John Macdonald laid down the policy of this party and of this country's long British policy. As I understand it, we are all together in this war. We do not know who will own the country before the next Dominion day arrives, because the whole empire and the dominions are being attacked now and are in very grave danger from the axis powers. As I say, we are in the war together, but sometimes some of the parties in the house seem to me to forget that particular fact. The object of some-it is not my object, but it is the object of some here-seems to be to use the great national danger in which we find ourselves to-day in order to advance what I might call the aims of their own political parties and their own political faiths. That is a great mistake, because nothing else matters until the war is won. It is our only business.
Speaking to the electors of the city of Kingston in December, 1844, Sir John Macdonald used these words with reference to the fiscal policy of the country as it was then:
I, therefore, need scarcely state my firm belief that the prosperity of Canada depends upon its permanent connection with the mother country, and that I shall resist to the utmost any attempt, from whatever quarter it may come, which may tend to weaken that union.
Forty-seven years afterwards, speaking in the same city in February, 1891, in his last campaign-he was again elected-Sir John reaffirmed the same doctrine of our close relationship with the mother country. He said:
For a century and a half this country has grown and flourished under the protecting aegis
of the British crown. Under the broad folds of the union jack, we enjoy the most ample liberty, we govern ourselves as we please, and at the same time we participate in the advantages which flow with association of the mightiest empire the world has ever seen. As for myself, my course is clear. A British subject I was born and a British subject I will die.
In the course of half a century, Sir John never failed to make the stand of Canada known, in its relation to the rest of the empire. In those troublesome days, before the fathers of confederation had drawn up the British North America Act, they all had to give and take, with the result that confederation was facilitated and thus brought about. Shortly before the last war Canada was the chief drifter from the mother country, of all the dominions, owing to status dream, isolation and separatism. The visit in May, 1939, three months before the war, showed the great popularity of the king and queen in their visit here, but the decline and decay of our parliamentary institutions had already set in, because of the fact that we had surrendered our rights and privileges and functions to bureaucratic boards of all kinds and to the executive, especially under the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). That is a serious mistake. To-morrow will be Dominion day and this week is called "army week." We had troops in front of these buildings to-night. I do not wish to speak with disrespect of the Minister of Finance, because I have a great deal of respect for every minister of the crown to-day in the laborious, thankless tasks they have, and whatever I shall have to say on the budget is said without any intention of giving offence to anyone and in a spirit of good-will. Indeed, I wish nothing but the utmost goodwill towards every member of the cabinet and this house. It seems to me, however, that the present Minister of Finance has forgotten the duty of this country to its soldiers at the present time. I have urged for three years that there should be some readjustment and reallotment of pay to the army, the navy and the air force. The question of pay was put through the house on September 10, in half an hour one night, Mr. Speaker-you were in the house-with practically no discussion at all. The present rates of pay were then established without discussion, and they have been found to be unjust, inequitable, unfair and full of inequalities; have done untold harm to recruiting and brought real hardship and suffering on soldiers' dependents. I find this every day in a soldier city from which I come.
A month ago I referred to what had been done in Washington, whereby every soldier in the United States army is given a minimum of $50 a month, with some receiving $60, and
The Budget-Mr. Church

extra pay all along the line. I was glad to receive some support in what I said then from my good friend the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght), and the soldier member for the Yukon (Mr. Black). I suggested that when these three payrolls were being discussed last session and this, they should be sent to some committee. In June, 1941, the present minister would not allow me to place on Hansard our schedules of pay, which are unjust and unfair, and nothing was done. I revived the matter this year. I venture to say that you could not get a Japanese office boy or cook to work for $50 a month, but what are we paying our men in uniform? It is all very well to sit and talk in this house; it is all very well to refer to what is being done on the farms and in the munitions plants, but that is as nothing compared with what is being done by our boys in the camps. Go to Camp Borden and the other camps throughout the country; see how our men sweat and toil all day. Yet all across the country this government has been spending money like water in the erection of camps, vast distances apart and at out-of-the way places, on expensive plants and military buildings. The youth of the city of Toronto have been taken from their homes and scattered all across the country, while the railways have been making millions of dollars out of the taxpayers, and this carnival of spending goes on. Down to the end of 1940, according to a return tabled in the house for me, the railways had made as much money as they made during the whole of the great war; yet they charge a soldier's wife or family $2 or $2.50 to go to Camp Borden to-morrow. The railways should be compelled to give the soldiers free transportation, particularly on holidays such as to-morrow, and on special occasions. We are becoming a laughingstock, the way we set one class of the community against another, and pay control boards and stay-at-home civilians and office soldiers in uniform, and refuse to pay those overseas and in training.
The plebiscite caused more dissension in Canada than has occurred at any other time in the history of our country. I believe the forgotten agency of the services of the government of the day is the army and one of the most necessary. It is the forgotten arm of the services. The cost of living bonus should be given to the dependents of those in the army, but it will never be given as long as the present state of affairs continues. I can tell you this, Mr. Speaker, that yes-men and nodders caused this war. The yes-men and nodders in Germany, Italy and Japan *brought about the tyranny and oppression

which exist in those countries, and caused the surrender and usurpation of the powers of the people to dictators, just as the House of Commons has surrendered its powers to controllers and bureaucratic boards. This House of Commons is to blame if the cost of living bonus is not given to soldiers' dependents and for Canada's bureaucracy of civil servants. Last fall a few small changes were made in the government's policy, but this added pin-money for a soldier bonus I think went to only about 204 people in military district No. 2, which at one time before the war had as many soldiers as all the rest of Canada combined. Many of these dependent people cannot pay their rent; some of them are without clothing and fuel, and this winter there will be a terrible condition. I think our schedules of pay should be brought up-to-date before we close. A committee should revise them, or I believe it can be done by the cabinet under the War Measures Act.
Then I suggest that the National Resources Mobilization Act should be enforced in regard to all classes of the community. I know of three young men in the city of Toronto, engaged in sports, who were given notice of their call last April. But they went away to a prairie town; then, against all regulations, they were allowed to join the air force, and now they are not to report to it until the end of August. In all other cases there is a thirty-day limit. How much longer are we [DOT] to continue a policy of this kind, while other young soldiers who are not earning extra money in sports, but for $1.30 a day are being killed every day over Germany? If that is the policy with regard to recruiting, there is no use in having an army week. The government's stand on sports in relation to the war should be made known. When we come to this building we find armed guards outside during this army week. But one-half of this building has been vacant since last June. If the government has no real war work to give the other branch of the legislature where there are so many able men of great experience ready to help, why not rent out that part of the building for an hotel, or use it to house some of our soldiers, or let it be used by some of these bureaucratic boards. The senate has been sent home, and the "House of Gordon" is reigning in its stead. I believe the time has come when we should stop talking about soldiers and do something practical about soldiers, who are going to defend this country from our enemies and fight the axis powers wherever found.
In my opinion, the budget simply deals with spending all along the line; there is

The Budget-Mr. Church
nothing in it about retrenchment or economy. It deals with the raising of $2,000,000,000 for the war. That matter has been debated here for months; but other than that there is very little new in the budget except provision for the cost of civil government, half a billion, and all that sort of thing, and marking up revenues from direct and indirect taxation. I believe the Minister of Finance should be compelled by statute law to bring down his budget on a fixed date each year. You, Mr. Deputy Speaker, have had a great deal of business experience through your legal connections in the city of Montreal, and you know that no large business concern of any kind could carry on as we carry on here. Six months of the year have passed and we have not yet had one dollar of our annual estimates passed in committee of supply. A haphazard budget is brought down, after several interim supply bills have been put through. From now on I am going to vote against every one of these interim supply bills as causing deficits and overdrafts. They are to blame for all the deficits we have in this country, war deficits, budget deficits and deficits on civilian estimates. The estimates do not contain the details. Any banking institution or insurance company which conducted its business as the Minister of Finance conducts his business on the present plan would close its doors in short order. I believe a date should be fixed by statute for the bringing down of the budget, and I also believe that we should establish a ways and means committee like the one at Washington. There are a great many inequalities in this new income tax schedule. These matters should come before a ways and means committee, as they do in the United States, because some of the professors and others advising the minister are not trained in business. On one occasion, referring to one of the unnamed government "spokesmen" talking over the radio, I described these people who are unnamed spokesmen, as the ghosts behind the scenes, because they tell us what we must do, but we do not know who they are. At Washington they have what they call a ways and means committee; they do not leave things to a bureaucratic board of officials. They take advantage, on such a committee, of the experience and knowledge of those who are in politics, who know something about questions of public policy and are trained in some form of competitive business. I do not believe any such income tax scheme would be imposed in that country. The minister has compared our income tax with the income tax in the United States, but he forgets that in the United States they have no sales tax,
and in England this year the income tax has not been raised. Also he charges too much to income and not enough to capital.
In this budget we have the highest income tax in the history of this country. I believe it is going to disrupt business to a great extent. I do not know how anyone is going to be able to pay his fixed charges for insurance, mortgage and other taxes. If a young man wants to get married, I do not know how he is even going to pay for any insurance or mortgage or keep his home. No small business man can pay all these fixed charges and the rest of the taxes out of the pin-money he will have left over after we pass this budget which has been drawn up by these bureaucratic powers over our heads. I believe the minister is taking too much from the taxpayers. There is no such thing as retrenchment in this budget. Look over the estimates, as I have looked over them four or five times from beginning to end, and can find no attempt at economy whatever. Do you see anything there about economy? Is there one word in the budget about economy? The civilian estimates have been brought before the house, but not one dollar has been passed yet-and let me point out that we have now reached the ninety-seventh day of the session. Not one dollar of estimates has been passed yet by this house.	'
That is the system we have in the house. If municipalities ran their affairs in that way they could not get along, and municipal governments would be beaten in their annual elections on the first of January. I say the system is all wrong, and it should be changed. This year the British budget was brought down on April 14 by Sir Kingsley Wood, and in that budget there is no increase in the income tax. The small man has his exemptions for dependants and those he has to keep. In Canada the only thing to do is to turn your business over to the state. And the state-this federal state *-is taking income and corporation taxes away from the municipalities and provinces and destroying the basis of confederation.
This all arises from that celebrated document known as the Sirois report. Ontario has become the goat of confederation, and under this particular budget she is most certainly the goat of confederation. When a comparison is made between this budget and the budget introduced in Washington, it will be found that the leading principles set out in the first part of our budget and review of the year are copied from Washington largely as to details and subject matter. That is all it is; it is a copy from Washington. I shall refer to it in more detail in a few moments.
The Budget-Mr. Church

No more interim supply should be passed until conditions are remedied. Hon. members are not doing their duty. Prior to the discussion on Bill No. 80, this House of Commons might as well have met in secret. When the public realizes that the important debates of their representatives in parliament are being held in secret they will have something to say about the whole matter.
The press have done well and at a great cost have given the people the facts. I am one who all along has advocated the removal of censorship barriers which have been placed in the way of the press. The present censorship should be abolished, because it is not a censorship at all. We would have no news only for the press, and not the radio. In England press censorship has been eliminated. They have eliminated so-called information bureaux. Before the censorship was removed in England the minister in charge of the information bureau there was in hot water almost every day, just like our own minister who heads our bureau of information. The fact that we call it an information bureau affords the only bit of humour in the whole session.
I say that press censorship as we have it at the present time should be abolished. The press should be free to publish the news. This information bureau with a pamphlet of its own, which hands out information, is only a farce because it gets its news from the newspapers. I sympathize with the newspapers when they do not publish proceedings of the house. One great newspaperman told me, before he died, that the proceedings are not worth publishing. Well, I am not prepared to go that far, because I believe this is the only place where the average man on the street or woman in a bus may have his or her grievances remedied. When we fail to function, parliamentary government is at an end. After all is said and done, the private member is the connecting link between the government of the day and the electors; and when he fails to function all parliamentary government is at an end. Are we going to wait until there is a rebellion of hon. members against this bureaucratic system of budgeting and surrender of our functions to all these czars and autocratic controls and boards costing the country millions?
I do not see any of the other Toronto members here to-night, and I do not care whether many members are here or not at present. But I want to say this, that the city of Toronto is the chief tax-paying city in the whole of the dominion. At one time they were paying between 25 per cent and 30 per cent of cash taxation of the dominion. This is the first time since confederation that that

great city has been without a single representative in the cabinet of the country, since 1935. We have one or two cabinet members from Ontario, but it seems to me they are not active enough to stand up for their province and prevent us from being burdened in this way. The city of Toronto has sent more recruits than any other centre, notwithstanding comparisons by tables, indexes, pamphlets and that kind of thing, and we have no direct cabinet representation as a city proper.
I am glad the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) is in his seat, and I would suggest to him that he turn to the fifteenth chapter of St. John and refer to the thirteenth verse where it says:
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
As thousands did in this and in the last war for our empire. I have a very high regard for the minister; he is a great lawyer, and a fine gentleman; but in his references to the British empire I believe he made a grave mistake, and it was a most unfortunate speech at this time. I can tell him that if the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) loses his seat in the city of Quebec, I believe he could get one in Ontario, or in the Toronto district, because he commanded a Toronto unit in the great war, and his name is much respected by soldiers in Ontario. I am glad to say that about him in his absence; he is not in his seat to-night. I say to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada that his speech of the other evening when he referred to the mother country was a most unfortunate one. Let him remember, on this eve before Dominion day, that 4,275 boys from Toronto lie buried in France. They went over there without compulsion; they enlisted as volunteers, and they will lie in France, where they died fighting the battles of this country, until the resurrection morning. There is no bigotry in Toronto or ill-feeling toward others in this confederation.
I believe the Minister of Justice was not in his seat when I referred earlier to Sir John A. Macdonald. Let him remember that I am a great admirer of what the French people did, along with Britain, for civilization. I respect what was done by the glorious land of France in the last war; I respect what they then did for the world and for civilization. They took part in the great war for their state, their religion, freedom and civilization generally, and Britain and France deserved a better fate than this war. I should hope that before another Dominion day comes along, that fine land of France may be rid forever of those savage barbarians who have invaded the

The Budget-Mr. Church
country, and it can be done only by Canada taking part in another peninsular war, by a total war effort.
I suggest that the Minister of Justice might go to the city of Quebec and read the inscription on the monument to the memory of Wolfe and Montcalm, an inscription which will last for all time, and which was there in the days of Sir John A. Macdonald. I have always believed in a policy for all the provinces of a confederation, and in the old Cornish battle cry: "Each for all and all for each."
This is what I said in the house on March 19 of last year:
We in Canada should be a united country from coast to coast. Wolfe and Montcalm lie buried together at Quebec, and the inscription on their monument attests the unity of the races in this country, as described in the motto on their memorials on the Plains of Abraham. Britain and Prance in the last war fought for a better world and for a better fate than has befallen them. I have always believed in the principles of confederation since I have been in this house-of the old Cornish battle cry of "Each for all and all for each". There is no use in our thinking that this is going to be an easy victory. We have no divine right to victory. This is going to be a most difficult, hard and heavy task and we should face that fact before it is too late. Facts are facts, and we should take our lessons from the past. So far we have lost the war and almost every battle; we have had no successes-
And we have lost the war so far right down to our Dominion day to-morrow. I say the same to-day.
A few days ago my good friend the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) referred "to my absentee leader". Let me say to him that our party polled nearly half the votes in the last election. The Right Hon. Arthur Meighen is a private citizen now. About him I would say that he is a great Canadian and Britisher, and I think he got a very dirty deal in the campaign which was conducted against him in a riding, near one which I used to represent a few years ago. In addition to that, as head of a city which had joint relations with the Township of York, it was under my regime that the municipal services were installed-roads, sewers, water, street cars and all that kind of thing there. Some of the people of Toronto and of York South did not approve the most unfair treatment given my former right hon. leader by certain people inside and outside the house. He has two sons now in England and ready to go to the continent. I regret that I do not see as much of him as I should like, and I do not believe I have had twenty words with him since he was defeated in February. But I was one of his followers here for many years, and I want
to say that he is a man who speaks his mind and says what he believes to be true. He represents, I believe, a large body of public opinion in this country, even though he did not win that election. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was beaten; Sir John Macdonald was beaten, and so were many others.
Many of those who are now talking here and elsewhere about reconstruction are the very people who were responsible for our being unprepared to fight this war. They said that we could depend upon the Monroe doctrine, the League of Nations, the Kellogg note, Locarno, pacifism, Geneva, the status quo, isolation and collective security. There is collective security only when there is an armed Britain. We were told that we could depend upon notes and pacifism and Geneva. The Minister of Finance is presenting his budget, but let me tell him that last week I received a return which shows that, all told, $6,000,000 of the taxpayers money was spent, without any protest from the minister, on this sham folly of the League of Nations. He was one of those who went to Geneva a year or two before the war. He became imbued with all these kinds of pacifist ideas even after Hitler had taken the ascendency in Germany. The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. O'Neill) also went to Geneva. I was glad to see them all go, because one of them told me after he came back that it was a wonderful trip, that it was a good cure for any ill health from which one might be suffering. Many of them made no report at all, but they said that the boats, hotels, meals, side-shows and cigars were good; that the banquets were wonderful and the wine perfect; that it was a delightful pastime attending the league and imbibing the doctrines that got us into this war.
This is the agency that caused the war, the league, Locarno, the Kellogg pact, pacifism, the Monroe doctrine, the status quo and pan-Americanism. Is it any wonder the taxpayer is groaning when he sits down and sees $6,000,000 spent on the league folly, $186,000 more this year, and that a million and a half of his money has been spent on the plebiscite mistake? If Hitler or Japan invade Canada, I said in my constituency, they would take the plebiscite and all connected with it and hang them on the sour apple tree alongside John Brown's body. The people of Canada, I find, are beginning to get quite bellicose against the present government and the House of Commons because of the plebiscite and because of the way they were led to believe that a vote for the plebiscite would be a vote for conscription and for a total war effort.
I can tell the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), that if it were not for the mother
The Budget-Mr. Church

country, after Dunkirk we would have had the enemy in the St. Lawrence, and they would have blown down the citadel and this building long before he was sworn in. Then Quebec would have had the police gestapo, the concentration camp, the whip, the loud speaker, the tramping of feet, the taking over to Germany of thousands to work there, the burying of men, women and children alive as has happened in Russia and Czechoslovakia. They would have had the slavery which is worse than death. It behooves the people, not only of Quebec but of all Canada to pay tribute to the mother country for protecting our shores ever since we have been a nation. If it were not for the work of the British fleet and the air force after Dunkirk, long ago Washington and Ottawa would have had to sue for peace with the axis powers, and we would have had slavery worse than death.
I believe the League of Nations was largely responsible for the fact that we were unprepared when this war came. Munich was necessary because it gave us a year's respite, and a respite was necessary because Britain and France, either singly or collectively, were no match for Hitler. They purchased a truce; they had to buy a truce for one year, which later became an ultimatum. But what did we do? We did nothing all that year but spend money in the old way to send deputations to the league and all that kind1 of thing, and refused to see the handwriting on the wall. The Prime Minister was in Berlin in 1937, and if he had kept his eyes open he would have seen those huge tanks on the streets of Munich, Berlin and other places. He should have come back and told the people what Germany was doing. The taxpayer will not forget all these things when he pays his tax bill to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) and the Minister of Finance under the present budget. This confiscatory budget is going to destroy all competitive business, large and small, in this country. In England1 they have passed a law known as the pre-war trade practices act which will restore the wholesaler and the retailer his pre-war trade practices. We are relying on different agencies here, and the bureaucrats will, in the end, drive this country into bankruptcy. If I had time I would read the remarks of the chairman of the wartime prices and merry-go-round board in Montreal that all competitive business was at an end.
There has been a great hip-hurrah over this budget from the press of this country, also from the paid officers and press agents that the government have hired and from other loud-speakers of civil servants and of their control boards all over the country. You can-
not pick up a newspaper without reading of these new controls ordered over our heads. The minister of the crown responsible for them all is the present Minister of Finance. The minister told me that he could not give me the cost of the ceilings. That was before Easter, but during the Easter recess the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board said in Winnipeg that it would be $2,000,000. Inside of two weeks the same civil servant, Donald Gordon, was announcing the information, over the heads of this parliament while it was in session, that the cost of the ceilings would be $2,000,000. What kind of recognition will we get from the electors? The minister has brought down an item of $50,000,000 for ceilings for these bureaucrats over our heads, but by next year it will be a quarter of a billion without any control by parliament.
There are a lot of Utopians in and out of this house who advocate various policies. As I see it, they have one thing in common. They have always in the past been mistaken; before the war they were mistaken about notes and collective security, about the Monroe doctrine, the status quo and pan-Americanism. If I had taken a stand like that, when I came to the House of Commons I would have taken the penitent's bench, because I would have felt that I was guilty and had been responsible for a budget like this, and for this war which may engulf civilization. But no, they go round the country now posing as super-patriots, and they tell us about the new utopia that there is going to be after the war. Remember the utopia we were promised after the last war- a land fit for heroes to live in-a war to end war? We all know what happened. Our heroes were forgotten. They said it was a war to end all wars, and they advocated then, as they are doing now, all kinds of nostrums and cures. They should wait to see whether we are going to win the war, because that must be done first. Nothing else matters. Although we have many domestic problems, we do not yet know to whom Canada will belong.
I wish to protest about the way the income tax is being carried out. It is going to abolish all competitive business, large and small. The small man is not treated fairly, and in other ways the budget is full of inequalities, injustices, hardships and pitfalls.
The government has appointed a horde of officials in connection with the wartime prices and trade board. I have a clipping here which says:
Ottawa, May 13.-Fred W. Jones, of London, Ontario, has been appointed director of the

The Budget-Mr. Church
management service section of the wartime prices and trade board's division of simplified practice.
The management service section plans to propose programmes that will aid the small business man to bring about economies in his operations, and re-model his methods to meet present-day problems caused by the price ceiling and merchandise shortages. Operations will be carried out by field consultants in various trade categories. Offices are located in Toronto and Montreal, advising the small man how to run his business.
We have a whole regiment of officials appointed, not many of whom ever had any connection with any retail or wholesale competitive business, or any business. I have'a list of some of them here, with their names and former occupations. If the war policy of the government, as I said last year, is to control and administer every walk of life and almost every article or commodity of trade and commerce, it is going to bring this country to disaster and national bankruptcy and will not help win the war. These bureaucrats and boards have certainly got business into a huge mess in this country. The ceilings are bound to collapse, because many of them are founded only on sand. Some of the ceilings on the necessaries of life were no doubt absolutely necessary perhaps last season, if they had been properly administered. If all these bureaucrats were necessary for the winning of the war, no one would object, but we should beware of this hidden evil, the bureaucracy within our gates, with headquarters at Ottawa. From birth to death we are registered and controlled, supervised, directed and even dragooned. You can be arrested and kept in gaol without trial, on the word of a minister advised by his civil servants. We can be taken from home and our work, and sent hither and thither up and down the country, without any appeal.
The Minister of Finance has put himself in control of these men behind the scenes- professors, economists and all that kind of thing. They tried to do that in England, but there was such a rebellion in the House of Commons there that they stopped it and corrected the errors and got some parliamentary control. The idea seems to be, "a board a day will keep Hitler away". A newfangled controller a day is transforming all Canada into a serfdom and destroying all chance of the small, independent business man to exist. We have overnight become a nation run by bureaucrats, many of whom have never had any practical business experience with competitive business, and under the pretext of war they coin out their utopian economic new-deal methods and patent medicines and quack remedies for the poor, dear, suffering public and give him a knockout blow.
The budget has not one word to say about the housing situation. The housing conditions in the industrial city from which I come are simply disgraceful, and housing conditions in this city of Ottawa are also very bad. But nothing has been done about that. No doubt this question of housing and the beef control farce will be pulled out of the refrigerator by Christmas and be administered when one of the large number of bureaucratic boards we have in this country allow it. There are few walks of life which are not now supervised or directed by some department of state at Ottawa.
People want the money that is to be raised for war purposes to go for war purposes, but half of this budget is not for war purposes at all. They want the war vigorously carried out, its costs distributed as fairly as possible and the general welfare put ahead of special interests. They want a suspension of disputes and no special favours toward anyone-farmers, capital, labour, social workers or anyone else. Let me quote what Mr. Winston Churchill said in the House of Commons on April 13, 1939, with respect to bureaucracy:
I know very well the patriotism and sincere desire to act in a manner of perfect rectitude which animates ministers of the crown, but I wonder whether there is not some hand which intervenes and filters down or withholds intelligence from ministers.
This budget is largely copied from the United States. The Minister of Finance, addressing the House of Commons a month ago, said:
In my judgment parliament is more and more on trial at the bar of public opinion. There is something wrong with the House of Commons. I am not reflecting on the house, and I do not know what is the cause, but there is something wrong with it. I have asked myself is this the fault of the government in any way?
Following that the Financial Post sent me a wire for an opinion and I replied:
What is wrong with Mr. Ilsley? Why doe? he not veto and apply the brakes to the orgy and wasteful expenditures and to the way a mint of money is being spent like water over parliament's head.
A civil war was fought in England for nearly one hundred years to gain control over expenditures and of the executive now surrendered to irresponsible boards and bureaucrats who mostly never had any training in any competitive business. The press will not report the proceedings of parliament, who might just as well meet secretly, yet pages of paper glorify sports. I propose that the annual budget be brought down on a fixed statutory day.
Over our heads, while parliament was sitting, a subsidy was announced by Mr. Donald Gordon, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, for fruit and vegetables. He announced to a delegation representing 25,000 Ontario fruit and vegetable growers that the
The Budget-Mr. Dechene

price ceiling would not be punctured to allow increased prices on produce grown for canning and jam processing industries. But he promised that the board would consider paying a subsidy on such products if processors and growers could prove to the board that the price of any one product should be increased. All that was done while parliament was in session 1 A huge amount has already been spent by the board in subsidies, and Mr. Gordon has surrounded himself with a lot of people who never were in business.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that I had to speak without any preparation, on such short notice.

subtopic: BEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in asking you for the privilege of the floor, may I say that I would not inflict myself upon this august assembly were it not that I am convinced that the matter I wish to discuss should be discussed in this budget debate because it relates to a part of our activities that is very much in the limelight at the moment.
First, however, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) upon the presentation of his budget some days ago. It strikes me that it was the most courageous budget ever presented, and the presentation itself was an outstanding performance because, while it presented requirements in such staggering amounts the minister made everybody like it. But as usual in all democracies those who have been yelling the loudest for total war are reluctant to congratulate the minister upon presenting a budget which undoubtedly means total war for all the people of Canada. At the other end of the line, strange as it may appear, those who have been agitating for the conscription of wealth, whatever that may mean in the present circumstances, those who have been asking that the rich be taxed, now appear to be dissatisfied because the rich are being taxed out of practically everything they make.
I believe, however, that the Canadian people as a whole, of all classes, will agree with the tribute I have feebly tried to express to the Minister of Finance for his masterly budget in these critical times.
I notice by the tariff schedules in the Votes and Proceedings of June 23 that the government proposes to remove entirely the duty on machinery used to separate oil from bituminous tar sands. I am speaking from memory, but I believe the old tariff was 27^ per cent. This is being taken off entirely, showing the gov-

ernment's intention to help in the development of these great resources of our north country.
I have a piece of information which I should like to give to this assembly. It came to me from the far north, a part of the country which liars have not reached yet; one generally gets the truth from the people there. A large amount of material is being moved by some important company to Fort Norman, some 900 miles north of Fort McMurray, with the purpose of constructing a pipeline from Fort Norman to White Horse to supply gasoline, oil and other petroleum products for use on the new highway being constructed by the United States government through the Yukon to Alaska. But on behalf of the people of Fort McMurray, which is right in the centre of the greatest field of bituminous tar sands in the world, bar none, as has been proved by outstanding engineers of this government, and others, I wish to protest to this house against the apparent neglect of these great resources which, after all, are so much closer to the transportation system of Alberta and of Canada generally. An engineer of the Department of Munitions and Supply, in making a report to that department some weeks ago, stated it was not advisable to expend any money in developing the tar sands of the Fort McMurray and Fort McKay areas because of their inaccessibility. He expressed that opinion in spite of the fact that the railway runs through fifty miles of these sands, right to the town of Waterways, and within a few miles of Fort McMurray, and in view of the further fact that the greatest armies of the world to-day are engaged in a most murderous and costly struggle for the control of certain oil resources. Hitler is willing to go a thousand miles and wade through an ocean of blood, leaving thousands of corpses on his way, in order to reach either the Caucasus or the Iran fields, while we in Canada declare that a field like the Fort McMurray area, only 350 miles from Edmonton, is too far away for us to consider.
Through the courtesy of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Sissons) who is always awake to anything in the interests of the far north, my attention has been drawn to the issue of the Canadian Geographical Journal of June, 1942. In that magazine I find an extremely well-written article, containing information in the possession of the Department of Mines and Resources, written by S. C. Ells, an engineer of such repute that his fame has gone far beyond the confines of the Dominion of Canada. Mr. Ells was one of the first, away back in 1913, to go down the Athabaska river from Athabaska Landing, at what is now the

The Budget-Mr. Dechene
town of Athabaska in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, to investigate these tar sands. He went down in a scow to investigate what he had heard from the voyageurs of the Hudson's Bay company and the missionaries about these great tar sand deposits along the Athabaska and Clearwater rivers. It may not be of any great interest to the house, but some hon. members have given a certain amount of attention to this subject, and I was surprised that so little is known about it. In 1904, nearly forty years ago, I myself went down the Athabaska river in a scow as far as Fort McMurray. Even in those days, at Pelican portage, near the House river, the Department of the Interior of those days had sent some engineers to investigate the possibilities of gas and oil in that part of the country. They dug a well at House river near Pelican rapids which struck such a tremendous flow of natural gas that for a great many years it could not be capped. In those days the machinery which can now be used to stop flows of that kind had not been invented. Fire was set to that flow of gas, and one could hear the noise of it about eight or ten miles away, while at night one could see the flames burning 150 feet in the air. It continued to burn for some years, until the force was spent, allowing the engineers to cap the well.
In those days I went to Fort McMurray and saw these tar sands. In some places they were over two hundred feet high; it was an impressive thing to see them shining in the sun. Since that time Mr. Max W. Ball and his associates at For McMurray spent over half a million dollars in the construction of a plant to mine and refine these sands successfully. It was not a share-selling proposition; they put up their own money.
The reason why I present these facts to the house to-night is to try to interest the government and the people of this country in order to see whether something cannot be done, at a time when we cannot get gas elsewhere, and in view of the fact that eminent engineers have expressed themselves as so favourable to development work. Mr. C., S. Bowey, of the United States bureau of mines, a man of outstanding repute, after investigating that field declares that it is the largest field of bituminous sands in the world and contains the largest oil reserves in the world. I am not speaking merely of America. In 1937 he estimated that the known field, which extends two hundred miles along the Athabaska and fifty miles along the Clearwater river, contains deposits, which he himself saw, from which could be extracted with the machinery available in those days-and which
has been improved since

two hundred and fifty billion barrels of oil, while the known resources of the rest of the world, barring what may have been discovered elsewhere since that time, are only some thirty-nine billion barrels. Yet everywhere in Canada we are cutting down the consumption of gas in order to carry on our war effort, while 350 miles by railroad and 245 miles by air from the city of Edmonton, there is an unlimited amount of gas and oil for the Canadian people to develop.
There is another aspect of this subject which I wish to mention to the Minister of Finance.
I have not had time to reckon the amount; but I venture to say that during the last few years, until we recently cut down consumption, the large amount of gasoline, crude oil, and oils of all sorts imported from the United States has had a great deal to do with the adverse balance of trade which affects our exchange with that country. Besides that, we are importing millions of barrels of crude oil from south America, or at least we were doing so until the Germans stopped us. We were importing that crude oil to be refined on the east and west coasts and in Montreal. Millions of dollars were involved, while our own resources in our own country, sufficient to supply the needs not only of Canada but of America, are lying practically idle.
To-night the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) referred to the treatment of mineral companies. I do not agree with the ideas he expressed in that regard. I say that when this war is over, contrary to what he seems to have in mind, whether it be a year or two or three years from now, we shall be facing a world which has wasted billions of tons of minerals of all kinds, blown up into the air, or sunk into the depths of the sea all over the world, to such a staggering extent that no man would dare to estimate the value of it. Besides the world scarcity of agricultural products, to be supplied by the great Canadian wheat lands, there will be a world scarcity of cattle and hogs, also to be supplied by the great western provinces and by the eastern provinces as well; and the demand for those products of this dominion, to replace the stocks of starving Europe and other parts of the world, will be tremendous, because there will be nothing left in the most populated parts of the globe. The war monster of Hitler will have eaten it all up. But just consider the wastage that is taking place in steel, iron, copper, aluminum, oil and everything else. All these commodities are being wasted, billions of tons and billions of dollars' worth of them. Canada with its
The Budget-Mr. Dechene

vast resources, in practically all these mineral fields, and with great coal resources, some of them untouched so far, will be able to supply the needs of the world. Take the coal resources in the Peace River country and the Rocky mountains, estimated at billions of tons-the best steam coal, available in Canada, but so far from communication that they are not being developed at present. This is in addition to the fields already in operation. Take the resources of Alberta alone. The coal resources of that province are estimated to be 15 per cent of all the coal of the British empire.

speechtext:
Yes, of the world. Then take our oil and other minerals. I suggest that if we begin now to consider the tremendous expenditures we have to make, and which I approve, in order to win the war; if we start now to organize for post-war production to replace the wastage that is at present taking place; if we develop these resources at Fort McMurray alone, for example, we shall be taking a step in the right direction. At Fort McMurray the possibilities are simply immense. According to the figures of the engineer of the Department of Mines and Resources-and he puts it lower than does the bureau of mines of the United States-the estimate is a hundred and fifty billion barrels. If we proceed to develop these vast resources, then within a few years after the close of the war the worries of the Minister of Finance will have ended. Just consider the tremendous wealth that will be produced. That is why I dare to rise in my place to-night and speak as I am doing.
Aristide Briand, the great foreign minister of the French republic after the last war, and one of the greatest men produced in that period-as hon. members will remember, he had dreams of the United States of Europe-made a remarkable statement with regard to the strategic advantage to the nation possessing the oil fields and oil resources of the world. He said that possession of these oil resources was the reason for the breaking up of peace conference after peace conference, economic conference after economic conference. He said that without these resources no nation could be great in times of peace. How much truer his words are to-day. No nation can become great, he said; no nation can go ahead and be powerful unless it possesses these vital resources so necessary to the machinery of transportation and to all the other operations of our modern age. This was one of the reasons for some serious misunderstanding between the British and French governments.
[Mr. Dechene.l
Though the French government obtained a mandate in Syria, all they saw of the oil resources was a pipeline going through the country. But do we need to have impressed upon us the fact that the possession of these oil resources is as important as Briand stated? Surely it is palpable, it is a truism, that no nation can go ahead without this possession. As he said, it has caused the breakdown of many peace conferences.
I say therefore that, no matter what other burdens we may have to carry, we should proceed with the development of these vast resources. There is no wild-catting about it. This year in the dominion, I venture to say, $1,000,000 or more will be spent in attempting to prove oil fields. Sometimes six thousand or seven thousand feet will be drilled at tremendous cost, and many times there will be a dry hole. That may be true of the Turner valley or other places, but at Fort McMurray there is no dry hole. There is the sand staring you in the face, and the statement has been made by Mr. Max W. Ball, who is operating in the field and has spent his own money, that in cutting walls through the sand, with a steam shovel, or with whatever tools they use, they strike ponds of clear bitumen. Everything that we have been importing from Trinidad and far-off places in the world we have in the far north. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, it is no longer the far north, because there is a railway right through the property.
On motion of Mr. Dechene the debate was adjourned.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
